nodes.title: Animal Welfare and Behavior Change
nodes.claim: High moral concern for animals coexists with behavior that causes extreme suffering.

nodes.title: Architecture, Aesthetics, and the Built Environment
nodes.claim: What makes a building (or designed object) good, and on what grounds do we judge styles legitimate or "fake"? Much aesthetic criticism smuggles in implicit norms — originality, "honesty," authenticity — that may not survive contact with the actual history of how things were built. And when we compare eras, we must be sure we are comparing like with like rather than a filtered remnant.

nodes.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Cognition
nodes.claim: Machine-learning systems have advanced faster than skeptics predicted, and the same capability that makes them useful makes them hard to control: capable goal-optimizers pursue proxies and instrumental power in ways their designers did not intend, while the systems remain opaque. The field's central tension is scaling capability and safety together, under competitive pressure to be first.

nodes.title: Culture and Politics of Progress
nodes.claim: Technological progress is shaped not only by economics and institutions but by culture and politics: how societies feel about progress, whom they blame for its costs, and whether the people building things participate in governing the places they build. Pessimism and risk-aversion can become self-fulfilling drags on progress.

nodes.title: Environmental Policy and Global Commons
nodes.claim: Environmental harms like ozone depletion and climate change are global commons problems — diffuse, "well-mixed," and requiring international cooperation. Most such efforts fail; the ozone success shows the conditions under which they can work.

nodes.title: Everyday Technology and Domestic Labor
nodes.claim: Much of human welfare — and especially women's — has been determined not by glamorous frontier technology but by the mundane tools of daily life: how food is processed, how households are run, how much time subsistence demands. This labor is economically invisible yet enormous, and the technologies that relieve it (and why they do or don't spread) are under-studied drivers of progress.

nodes.title: Existential Risk and Long-Run Growth
nodes.claim: Technological progress both creates the risks that could end civilization and supplies the wealth and capability to manage them. The central question is whether, over the long run, growth raises or lowers humanity's chance of survival — and what that implies for how much we should slow down "for safety."

nodes.title: Fertility and Demographic Change
nodes.claim: Fertility has fallen below replacement across the developed world, driving population aging and decline. This threatens the flow of new people (and new ideas) and tilts societies toward risk-aversion — yet much of the decline reflects removable barriers and a mispriced public good, not settled preferences.

nodes.title: Finance, Markets, and Technological Progress
nodes.claim: How financial markets, capital allocation, and belief shape which technological futures get built. Prices aggregate expectations, speculative capital funds (and miscodes) the future, and ambitious firms use monopoly and conviction to make long-shot bets viable.

nodes.title: Health, Medicine, and the Body
nodes.claim: Why some conditions of the body resist treatment while others yield, what makes an intervention durable, and why some health needs go chronically unmet. Many bodily outcomes are products of regulated systems shaped by evolution; and which problems get solved depends on funding, ethics rules, and who does the research.

nodes.title: Housing and Urban Land Use
nodes.claim: Productive cities have made housing scarce and expensive through land-use regulation, pricing workers out of the places they would be most productive. The result is a national drag on growth and a political-economy trap in which the people who could authorize new building are those who benefit from not doing so. Credit conditions, tax policy, and height regulation overlay the supply picture and can obscure it.

nodes.title: Human Decision-Making and Behavioral Science
nodes.claim: How should we model human decision-making? The dominant rational-actor model is contradicted by a sprawling list of "biases," but cataloguing deviations has not produced a successor theory. The field's problem is to move from a collection of anomalies to a unified, predictive account of how minds actually decide.

nodes.title: Innovation Systems and Institutional Design
nodes.claim: How societies organize institutions to produce sustained, high-impact innovation.

nodes.title: Macroeconomic Policy and Public Finance
nodes.claim: How governments should tax, borrow, and spend — and when high public debt is or isn't dangerous. Public intuition tracks the level of debt, but the economics turns on burden (interest vs growth), the temporary-vs-permanent nature of spending, and finite fiscal capacity.

nodes.title: Maintenance, Reliability, and Failure
nodes.claim: Complex artefacts and systems decay and break under continuous stress; whether they survive depends less on their peak performance than on how they are prepared, simplified, and maintained. The field asks what makes a system reliable and repairable, and why upkeep is chronically undervalued relative to novelty.

nodes.title: Megaproject Delivery and Cost
nodes.claim: Ambitious public and scientific projects (telescopes, launch systems, infrastructure) routinely cost far more, take far longer, or never get built at all relative to what they should. The binding constraint is often not physics or funding but how the project is procured, contracted, timed against falling input costs, or politically sustained against localized opposition.

nodes.title: Metascience and Research Quality
nodes.claim: The institutions and incentives that fund and publish science do not reliably select for true, useful, or innovative findings. Symptoms — irreproducibility, slowing innovation, and declining research productivity — are often treated as separate problems, or as inevitable, but may share roots in how research is rewarded, staffed, and located.

nodes.title: Psychiatric Theory and Mental Disorder
nodes.claim: Psychiatry lacks a stable, explanatory framework for distinguishing disorder, dysfunction, and difference.

nodes.title: State Capacity and Economic Development
nodes.claim: Many low-income countries are trapped by low state capacity, not lack of ideas.

nodes.title: State Capacity Under Crisis
nodes.claim: How epidemics reveal the interaction between state institutions, civil society, and entrenched political economy constraints.

nodes.title: State Formation and Capacity Building
nodes.claim: How states escape low-capacity equilibria characterized by delegation, bargaining, and corruption.

nodes.title: Violence, Norms, and Social Order
nodes.claim: How societies without centralized courts or an overwhelming state monopoly on force manage the ever-present risk that interpersonal conflict escalates into unbounded or lethal violence — and how the rituals, conventions, and institutions that emerge to bound violence adapt as weapons, technology, and social structure change.

nodes.title: A Bet Prices the Cost of Being Wrong
nodes.claim: Where asserting a claim costs nothing, false and exaggerated claims proliferate because their authors bear none of the consequences of being wrong. Attaching a financial stake to an assertion imposes a price on error, which both deters the assertion of things the speaker does not actually believe and separates sincere conviction from performance. As Alex Tabarrok puts it, a bet is a tax on bullshit.

nodes.title: A Binding Constraint's Timing Collides With a Competing Demand
nodes.claim: A forced trade-off arises when the narrow window for one essential activity coincides with the peak demand of another, so both cannot be satisfied at once.

nodes.title: A Bright-Line Rule Persists Because It Limits Liability
nodes.claim: An over-conservative standard can be defended by the very firms it burdens, because a clear regulatory line caps their legal liability, giving incumbents a reason not to challenge it even when it is costly.

nodes.title: A Cartel Fractures When Members' Interests Diverge
nodes.claim: A coalition holds only while members' economic interests align; once external change makes those interests diverge, defection unravels it — the fall reflects divergence, not disloyalty.

nodes.title: A Certification Vacuum Blocks Adoption of a Working Technology
nodes.claim: The absence of an authoritative product-standard or efficacy certification can block the adoption of a technology that works, because buyers cannot distinguish good products from junk and so will not pay for either.

nodes.title: A Cognitive Paradigm Spreads Through Schooling and Textbooks
nodes.claim: A transferable way of thinking — not a physical artifact — diffuses through a population as a cultural trait carried by educational institutions and printed instructional materials, and can be tracked directly through them.

nodes.title: A Coherent Aesthetic Ideology Can Override Economic Incentives
nodes.claim: A coherent ideology about what things should look like can persuade decision-makers to abandon an affordable, available good, showing that culture is not merely downstream of technology and cost.

nodes.title: A Collection of Anomalies Is Not a Theory
nodes.claim: Cataloguing ever more deviations from a model you know is wrong is not scientific progress; a growing list of "exceptions" is a signal that the underlying model should be replaced, not patched. You need a new theory, not a longer errata.

nodes.title: A Community of Practitioners Disciplines a Science
nodes.claim: An outside community of "users" who apply a field's findings disciplines that field: they perform de facto replication (because products must actually work), force competing theories to reconcile when translated into practice, and champion useful ideas from outside the dominant paradigm. The relative absence of such practitioners worsens the social sciences' replication crisis.

nodes.title: A Complex System That Works Evolved From a Simple One That Worked
nodes.claim: A complex system that works is almost always found to have grown from a simple system that worked; a complex system designed whole from scratch does not work and cannot be patched into working (Gall's law).

nodes.title: A Concentrated Cache Yields Disproportionate Returns Over Scattered Finds
nodes.claim: A single intact repository can contribute more to a field than many isolated fragments, because value scales with completeness and coherence, so discovering one dense archive is a step-change rather than an increment.

nodes.title: A Continuously-Applied Fix Rebounds If Stopped
nodes.claim: An intervention that only suppresses a problem while continuously applied produces a rapid rebound if it stops, because the underlying driver was never removed and reasserts itself once the suppression ends.

nodes.title: A Corroborating Source Shifts Belief Between Competing Accounts
nodes.claim: When two conflicting records disagree, the discovery of an independent third source can decisively tip credence toward the previously distrusted account, because evidence is weighed comparatively.

nodes.title: A Credible Commitment Anchors Expectations and Lowers Enforcement Cost
nodes.claim: When the public believes an authority will hit its announced target, people build that belief into their own decisions, which stabilises the outcome and reduces the force the authority must actually apply.

nodes.title: A Discovery Waits for Its Enabling Technology
nodes.claim: An idea can be correct yet uncitable and untestable until the instruments or techniques needed to verify or exploit it exist.

nodes.title: A Dominant User Can Capture a Shared Commons
nodes.claim: When one user of a shared resource imposes large externalities on the others, it can drive them out entirely -- capturing a commons that once served a diverse mix, not by formal exclusion but by making shared use unsafe or unpleasant for everyone else.

nodes.title: A Drug Hitting Many Diseases Hints at a Shared Upstream Cause
nodes.claim: When one intervention independently improves a wide spread of otherwise-unrelated conditions, it suggests it may act on a common upstream process rather than on each disease separately.

nodes.title: A Field Advances Only Once It Can Collect Data
nodes.claim: A discipline leaps forward only after it acquires the infrastructure to collect standardised performance data; without it, practice stays speculative regardless of talent.

nodes.title: A Finding Is Inert Without a Theory or Use to Interpret It
nodes.claim: Even a well-characterized result stays dormant when the community has no framework or application that gives it meaning.

nodes.title: A Fixed Exchange Rate Forces Adjustment Onto the Domestic Economy
nodes.claim: Without a floating currency to absorb a trade deficit, a government defending a peg must repress domestic demand and credit, transmitting external pressure directly into the home economy.

nodes.title: A Forgiving Design Beats a Higher-Ceiling One When Operators Vary
nodes.claim: A method tolerant of variation in inputs and technique can deliver better real-world results than a more sensitive method with a higher peak, once inconsistent or unskilled operators are doing the work.

nodes.title: A Gene Drive Biases Inheritance to Spread a Trait Regardless of Fitness
nodes.claim: A genetic element that copies itself onto its partner chromosome is inherited by nearly 100 percent of offspring instead of the normal 50 percent, so it can sweep through an entire population even when it confers no advantage - or a disadvantage - to its carrier.

nodes.title: A Good's Decline Amid Falling Costs Implicates Demand, Not Supply
nodes.claim: When a good disappears even as it becomes cheaper to supply, the cause lies in what buyers want, not in what industry can produce.

nodes.title: A Group That Opts Out of One Input Isolates the Effect of the Others
nodes.claim: A community that deliberately rejects one component of a bundle of simultaneous changes, while accepting the rest, functions as a natural control group. Comparing its outcome with the general population identifies whether the rejected component was necessary - something no observational study of the general population can do, because there the components always move together.

nodes.title: A Guaranteed Purchase Contract Unlocks Third-Party Project Finance
nodes.claim: A binding promise to buy future output gives lenders the evidence of revenue they need to finance a supplier's capital-intensive buildout, so the demand guarantee multiplies its own effect by mobilizing outside debt and equity.

nodes.title: A Human-Machine Pair Co-Adapts Through a Feedback Loop
nodes.claim: Performance in a brain-computer interface comes from the user and the decoder each learning the other, so building the correction signal into ordinary use makes the joint system continuously self-improving.

nodes.title: A Ladder of Substitutes Means Solving the Top Rung Barely Moves the Aggregate
nodes.claim: When a visible problem is the tip of a graded ladder of substitutes, an intervention targeting only the visible rung leaves the much larger population one step down untouched.

nodes.title: A Large Enough Output-to-Input Ratio Makes the Input's Own Footprint Negligible
nodes.claim: When a process delivers far more of a good than it consumes in producing it, the purity of the input stops mattering. A remediation or production process with a sufficiently lopsided ratio need not be run on clean inputs to be worth running, because the input's own cost is a small fraction of the output.

nodes.title: A Manager's Override Rescues a Project the Consensus Would Kill
nodes.claim: Research consensus systematically undervalues high-variance projects near their breakthrough, so a single authority willing to overrule a majority vote - and to tolerate internal friction against a maverick - can be the decisive factor in whether the payoff is ever reached.

nodes.title: A Material's Value Can Lie in Its Programmed Disappearance
nodes.claim: Engineering a material to degrade harmlessly on a predictable schedule is often more valuable than making it permanent, because controlled resorption removes the need for a later removal or disposal step.

nodes.title: A Monopoly Regulator Produces No Comparison Class for Its Own Rules
nodes.claim: Where a single agency sets the rules for an entire domain, there is no parallel regime to compare it against, so its stringency cannot be shown to be excessive or insufficient. The absence of a comparison class is what makes a regulatory regime unfalsifiable and therefore unreformable.

nodes.title: A Palliative Risks Displacing the Underlying Fix
nodes.claim: A treatment that relieves a symptom can erode the will to address the underlying cause, so a genuine palliative risks becoming a substitute for the real fix rather than a complement to it.

nodes.title: A Phantom Technical Barrier Blocks a Cheap Fix
nodes.claim: A false belief about technical incompatibility can stall an otherwise simple and cheap transition for decades, until someone dispels the myth.

nodes.title: A Predictively Useful Model Need Not Be a Correct One
nodes.claim: A model can be false about the underlying mechanism and still be worth holding, provided it generates predictions that reliably narrow the search or guide action within the range being worked in. Practical value and truth are separable properties of a model.

nodes.title: A Prevailing Theory Can Wrongly Deem a Feasible Result Impossible
nodes.claim: A misapplied or over-extended theory can lead reviewers and scientists to dismiss an achievable outcome as physically impossible, starving it of support until someone pursues the 'impossible' case and reveals the theory was applied to the wrong variable.

nodes.title: A Price Cap Traded for Front-Loaded Subsidy Bridges to a Self-Sustaining Market
nodes.claim: Paying suppliers an early premium in exchange for a binding long-term price ceiling lets a subsidy end once marginal cost falls to buyers' willingness to pay, structuring the support as a temporary bridge rather than a permanent transfer.

nodes.title: A Prize Contest Mobilizes Distributed Effort on a Hard Problem
nodes.claim: Offering cash prizes for a well-specified breakthrough recruits many independent competitors whose parallel efforts can crack a problem faster than a single funded team, by paying for the output rather than the inputs.

nodes.title: A Product Category Fragments When Buyers Learn to Value Origin and Variety
nodes.claim: Once buyers stop treating a good as an undifferentiated commodity and start valuing its specific provenance and variation, demand splinters into many niche variants that the old high-volume production system was never built to serve.

nodes.title: A Project Pipeline Justifies Building In-House Capacity
nodes.claim: A continuous stream of projects makes it worth building and retaining a skilled in-house delivery team, which learns across projects, rather than renting consultants for each one-off.

nodes.title: A Proliferating Model Signals the Wrong Framework
nodes.claim: When a model needs ever more patches and special cases to fit the evidence, the proliferation itself is a signal the framework is wrong, because a correct model explains more with fewer rules.

nodes.title: A Regulator That Both Promotes and Polices Loses Public Trust
nodes.claim: When one body both develops and regulates a technology, its conflict of interest and instinct to downplay problems radicalise critics and ultimately destroy its credibility — and the technology's.

nodes.title: A Reproduction Technology Multiplies a Superior Unit's Reach
nodes.claim: A technology that copies or distributes a superior individual multiplies how many offspring or outputs it can produce, amplifying the returns to identifying the best.

nodes.title: A Scheme That Starves Local Revenue Loses Its Local Sponsor
nodes.claim: When a development scheme strips the local government of the tax revenue that funds the infrastructure new density requires, local authorities turn against it regardless of its other merits.

nodes.title: A Screened, Filtered Population Lowers Disorder Independent of Density and Diversity
nodes.claim: Order in a dense, diverse setting can come from screening and credible ejection of bad actors rather than from low density or homogeneity, isolating selection as the driver of safety.

nodes.title: A Self-Propagating Solution Beats One Requiring Continuous Reapplication
nodes.claim: An intervention that spreads and sustains itself through a system dominates one that must be manufactured and reapplied indefinitely, because the recurring version's cost never ends and scales with the area it must cover.

nodes.title: A Self-Transporting Medium Halves Infrastructure Needs
nodes.claim: A working medium that moves itself by its own physics needs less supporting infrastructure than one that must be actively pumped, a residual advantage that can keep an older system alive in niches.

nodes.title: A Single Design Parameter Can Cap an Entire System's Density
nodes.claim: One binding design rule can ceiling a whole system's density regardless of other choices, so adjustments elsewhere barely move the outcome.

nodes.title: A Single Measurement Mobilizes Political Will
nodes.claim: Producing the first local data on a hidden problem can convert latent, abstract concern into concrete government action, because a specific number about one's own population is far more motivating than a global estimate.

nodes.title: A Small Fraction of High-Ability Individuals Drive Most Breakthroughs
nodes.claim: Contribution to scientific and technological breakthroughs is extremely concentrated in a small number of exceptionally high-ability individuals, so factors that reduce their number or divert their effort elsewhere have outsized effects on aggregate progress that cannot be offset simply by adding more averagely-able researchers.

nodes.title: A Small Number of Persistent Offenders Drives Most Victimization
nodes.claim: The burden of offending is highly concentrated in a few prolific actors, so detecting and incapacitating a handful of them produces disproportionate drops in local harm.

nodes.title: A Solved Problem Becomes a Transferable Playbook
nodes.claim: Once rich countries have solved a problem, the solution can become a cheap, copyable playbook for everyone else, because the hard work of discovery is done and only application remains.

nodes.title: A Standardized Machine Can Outperform a Skilled Human on Consistency
nodes.claim: Because it repeats identical actions and holds key physical variables fixed, an automated process can beat expert manual execution on average output quality by eliminating the variance that human hands introduce.

nodes.title: A State That Values a Territory Governs It Better Than an Extractive One
nodes.claim: Cities matched to states that care about them — for ideological, religious, or nationalistic reasons — grow faster than under rulers seeking only tribute.

nodes.title: A Substitute Technology Neutralizes Coercive Leverage
nodes.claim: A technology that gives dependents an alternative source of a controlled resource neutralizes the controller's coercive leverage, turning a zero-sum dependence into a positive-sum situation.

nodes.title: A Successful Treatment Forecloses Study of Its Alternatives
nodes.claim: Once a "good enough" intervention exists, providers are obliged to give it to everyone who needs it, destroying the control group and making rival treatments hard to study.

nodes.title: A Superseded Technology Returns When Its Replacement Hits Limits
nodes.claim: A technology abandoned in favour of a superior substitute can become valuable again once the substitute runs into its own limits, reviving a tool that once looked obsolete.

nodes.title: A Targeted Mandate Survives Where a Universal One Provokes Coordinated Backlash
nodes.claim: Top-down mandates succeed when confined to limited areas that leave most voters unaffected, but provoke coordinated, election-deciding backlash when applied everywhere at once.

nodes.title: A Tax Base Too Narrow for Its Obligations Forces Structural Breakdown
nodes.claim: When a government's spending obligations grow far beyond its narrow tax base, the mismatch forces fiscal breakdown regardless of how the base is tweaked.

nodes.title: A Tax Meant to Free Idle Assets Can Instead Suppress Their Production
nodes.claim: A tax intended to force idle assets into use can, if badly designed, instead fall on producers and suppress the very activity it meant to encourage.

nodes.title: A Transport Speed Threshold Unlocks Distant Supply
nodes.claim: Crossing a threshold transit speed lets a perishable good arrive intact from distant producers, collapsing its price by opening cheap remote supply.

nodes.title: A Uniform Metric Ignores Differences in Value
nodes.claim: Allocating by a single uniform unit treats unlike things as identical, ignoring differences in value, cost, and need, and so systematically misallocates.

nodes.title: A Visible Success Shifts Public Expectations and Creates Demand
nodes.claim: Once people see that a public good is achievable, they come to expect and demand it, converting a possibility into a standard that institutions must meet.

nodes.title: Abandoned Technologies Return When Constraints Shift
nodes.claim: A technology sidelined because a rival was cheaper or easier can return decades later when the constraint that favored the rival changes -- the old approach was never inferior on every dimension, only on the ones that mattered under the old conditions.

nodes.title: Abating Harm Where It Is Cheapest Beats Abating It On-Site
nodes.claim: When a diffuse environmental harm can be offset anywhere within the affected system, requiring each project to neutralize its own contribution on its own site buys less protection per pound than letting the project pay for abatement wherever abatement is cheapest. Marginal abatement costs differ enormously across sources, so tying mitigation to the location of the harm forecloses the cheapest available reductions.

nodes.title: Absence of Central Authority Raises Homicide via Missing Dispute Resolution
nodes.claim: Without judges, police, or a central authority to resolve disputes, individuals resort to self-help, keeping within-group killing high even where organised warfare is rare.

nodes.title: Absence of Externalities Removes the Constituency for Restriction
nodes.claim: Where an activity imposes no concentrated local harm, no affected population forms to demand the restrictions that throttle onshore projects.

nodes.title: Absent Demand, Not Prohibition, Explains a Missing Market
nodes.claim: When a product is legal but scarce, and remains scarce even in jurisdictions where it is fully permitted, the binding constraint is lack of demand rather than regulation.

nodes.title: Abstraction Signals Unreliability
nodes.claim: The more abstract and nebulous the construct a study claims to measure (happiness, generosity, "priming," motivation), the more vulnerable its findings are to abuse and the less they should be trusted; concrete, time- and place-bound claims are comparatively safe.

nodes.title: Abundance Is a Neutral Substrate for Plural Ends, Not a Prescribed Lifestyle
nodes.claim: Progress recovers its appeal when it supplies a common material foundation on which many incompatible versions of the good life can be pursued, rather than prescribing one ideal future.

nodes.title: Academic Incentives Reward Novelty Over Scalability
nodes.claim: Publication and media attention flow to one-off demonstrations of a headline property, so researchers optimise for new discoveries rather than for whether a material can ever be produced at scale.

nodes.title: Access Rationing Reveals Undersupply, Not Prestige
nodes.claim: When a valuable resource is chronically over-subscribed and hard to enter, the scarcity is a symptom of unmet demand that scaling or public provision should fill, not a badge of exclusivity to be preserved.

nodes.title: Accessibility of a Style Is Independent of Its Age
nodes.claim: The property that makes a style broadly appreciable is not that it is old. Age correlates with accessibility for contingent historical reasons, so defending old styles as such defends the wrong variable and rules out new styles that would serve the same purpose.

nodes.title: Accessibility Requires Comprehensibility, Not Just Availability
nodes.claim: Removing formal access barriers does not achieve genuine access if the content remains too difficult to read; language itself is a barrier as real as a paywall.

nodes.title: Accessible Symbolic Goals Crowd Out Inaccessible Substantive Ones
nodes.claim: When most participants cannot contribute to a hard substantive problem, institutional attention flows to an accessible adjacent problem - often a visible symbolic or fairness goal - which can crowd out and even undermine the primary objective.

nodes.title: Accidental Failures Reveal Unsuspected Material Properties
nodes.claim: A tool that fails unexpectedly during routine use can expose a property no one was looking for, redirecting a research program.

nodes.title: Accommodating Stated Objections Fails When They Proxy for Local Self-Interest
nodes.claim: When the reasons people give for opposing something are not the reasons they actually oppose it, a reform designed to satisfy the stated objection will fail — the same people will object again on new grounds, because the underlying interest is untouched.

nodes.title: Accountability Gaps Let Systematic Errors Persist
nodes.claim: When many organizations each handle a slice of a process but none is accountable for the end result, systematic errors go uncaught because catching them is no single actor's job; assigning one accountable owner closes the gap.

nodes.title: Accurate Information Corrects Biased Perceptions of Social Norms
nodes.claim: People systematically misjudge how common or how disapproved a behaviour is; supplying accurate descriptive norms shifts self-reported behaviour toward the true norm.

nodes.title: Adapting a Foreign Component to the Host Prevents Rejection
nodes.claim: A component imported from one system into another is rejected unless it is adapted to resemble the host, so disguising the foreign part as native is what makes transplantation work.

nodes.title: Adapting Old Infrastructure Beats Building New
nodes.claim: Upgrading or recombining existing infrastructure through a small marginal investment often delivers more transport value per dollar than building an entirely new system, even when the existing assets are more than a century old.

nodes.title: Administrative Cost Can Exceed the Revenue a Tax Raises
nodes.claim: A tax can cost more to assess and administer than it collects, so that levying it loses the state money on net.

nodes.title: Adoption Requires the Skill to Reach the People Who Do the Work
nodes.claim: A tool with high latent potential lies dormant until basic competence in it penetrates the specific class of practitioners who actually execute the task, not just elite theorists.

nodes.title: Adverse Selection Suppresses Trade When All Counterparties Are Informed
nodes.claim: A proposed trade signals that the initiator may hold private information, so a rational counterparty declines, and in a market of only informed participants volume collapses toward zero.

nodes.title: Agglomeration Concentrates Innovation
nodes.claim: Innovative activity concentrates in a few geographic locations because co-location raises the productivity of the people doing it: proximity multiplies knowledge spillovers, sustains deep specialized labor markets, and creates a social scene where the best conversations in a field happen face-to-face. The cluster produces more than the sum of its firms.

nodes.title: Aggregate Rates Diverge From Individual Risk Factors
nodes.claim: The factors that predict which individual falls into a bad state can be uncorrelated with, or opposite to, what predicts the rate of that state across places.

nodes.title: Aggregating a Crowd Costs More Than Paying One Expert
nodes.claim: Buying wisdom-of-crowds through a subsidised market means paying many participants to show up, whereas a forecast can be bought by paying a single expert team, so subsidies are an expensive way to purchase accuracy.

nodes.title: Aging Populations Become Risk-Averse and Short-Termist
nodes.claim: As a society's median age rises, its politics and culture tilt toward the interests and dispositions of the old: more spending on pensions and care, less appetite for risk and long-horizon investment, and weaker constituency for multigenerational problems.

nodes.title: Aging Systems Raise the Cost of Working Around Their Accumulated Layers
nodes.claim: The longer infrastructure accretes, the more embedded services must be relocated for surface excavation, making trench methods progressively more expensive relative to going beneath.

nodes.title: Aligned Producer Incentives Enable Global Agreements
nodes.claim: Global collective-action problems become solvable when the actors with the power to act also have the most to gain from solving them — and when blocking incumbents can be turned into backers. Where those incentives are flipped (the powerful gain from the status quo), agreement is far harder.

nodes.title: Aligning Authority at One Accountable Tier Enables Delivery
nodes.claim: Concentrating planning, funding, and construction powers in a single accountable body lets one decision-maker own a project end to end, rather than diffusing responsibility across tiers.

nodes.title: Aligning Incumbent Incentives Enables Reform
nodes.claim: Reforms succeed when they let the incumbents who would otherwise block them share in the gains — converting potential opponents into supporters — rather than imposing concentrated losses on them.

nodes.title: Aligning the Windfall With the Veto-Holder Converts Opponents Into Advocates
nodes.claim: When the people who can block development are made the direct financial beneficiaries of it, their incentive flips from obstruction to advocacy.

nodes.title: All-or-Nothing Policy Rollout Forgoes Learning
nodes.claim: Governments and agencies tend to roll out policy in an all-or-nothing fashion across the whole system at once, rather than via incremental or randomized pilots — forgoing the chance to learn what works before committing everyone to it.

nodes.title: Ambitious Firms Make Technology Risk Conditional
nodes.claim: A sufficiently ambitious firm lowers its effective risk by aiming to be the only way a given technology can happen: this converts independent, multiplicative long-shot probabilities into conditional ones, compresses the range of outcomes, and confers the pricing power needed to make the technology profitable.

nodes.title: Ambitious Targets Are Cheap to Offer When Payment Is Contingent on Success
nodes.claim: A commitment that pays only on delivery costs nothing if the target proves impossible. Offering one for an apparently unreachable goal is therefore close to a free option, and the systematic preference for modest, confidently achievable targets forfeits large expected value for no saving.

nodes.title: An Acquirer Can Foreclose a Market by Withdrawing a Product Into Internal Use
nodes.claim: When a firm buys the maker of an enabling product and restricts it to internal use, it can destroy the wider ecosystem and reputation that made the product valuable, subtracting value from the market rather than adding it.

nodes.title: An Anchor Buyer Catalyzes a Coalition of Followers
nodes.claim: Securing one committed early buyer creates momentum that recruits peer organizations who would not move first, reducing a mass-coordination problem to the tractable task of finding a single first mover.

nodes.title: An Animal Model Is a Precondition for Systematic Biomedical Research
nodes.claim: Until a tractable animal model of a disease exists, research on it cannot proceed systematically: hypotheses cannot be tested cheaply, candidates cannot be screened, and results cannot be replicated. The search for a model is therefore not preliminary to the research programme, it is the rate-limiting step of it.

nodes.title: An Artificial Currency Brings Price Signals to a Non-Market Good
nodes.claim: Issuing a purpose-built token that participants spend in auctions can bring the information and efficiency of prices to a good that cannot or should not be bought with real money.

nodes.title: An Engineered Substitute Can Beat the Natural Original on Consistency and Cost
nodes.claim: Applying technical or culinary science can produce a synthetic stand-in that matches the key functional property of a natural input while improving on consistency, shelf life, and resource use.

nodes.title: An Ideology of Innovation Spreads by Imitation
nodes.claim: A culture of tinkering — the belief that anything can be improved by experiment — spreads from person to person by example: people become more willing to innovate when they see others doing it and succeeding. Copying, not original invention, is the basic human skill that propagates the habit.

nodes.title: An Intermediate Target Fails When Its Link to the Goal Breaks
nodes.claim: Steering by a proxy (the money supply) instead of the true objective (inflation) works only while the proxy's relationship to the goal is stable; when that link breaks, hitting the proxy no longer delivers the goal, and targeting the outcome directly becomes more robust.

nodes.title: An Internal Champion Moves an Organization Toward an Atypical Commitment
nodes.claim: Large organizations adopt unusual, expensive commitments only when an insider advocates for them from within, so outreach must find and equip internal champions rather than pitch the organization from outside.

nodes.title: An Offsetting Effect Masks the True Size of a Problem
nodes.claim: A second effect that happens to offset a problem can hide its true magnitude, so the problem looks smaller than it is until the offset is removed and the full size is suddenly revealed.

nodes.title: An Outcome That Cannot Be Measured Cannot Be Proven
nodes.claim: An intervention whose benefit cannot be measured in the real world cannot prove itself, so it stalls regardless of whether it works, because trials come back underpowered or confounded.

nodes.title: An Unfakeable Signal Requires the Signaled Good Be Costly to Obtain
nodes.claim: A status signal only works while the signalling good is genuinely hard and expensive to obtain; ease of acquisition destroys its ability to certify wealth.

nodes.title: An Unfalsifiable Theory Survives on Elegance Rather Than Evidence
nodes.claim: When a theory's central variable can be operationalized in many defensible ways, the literature will contain both supportive and unsupportive results whatever the truth, and no accumulation of studies can settle it. The theory then persists on intuitive appeal, and its survival is evidence about its elegance rather than about the world.

nodes.title: Antitrust Changes Innovation Incentives
nodes.claim: Antitrust policy shapes not just market concentration but firms' incentives to invest in long-term research, because limiting scale, forcing divestiture or reducing vertical integration also reduces the expected returns from work that only pays off at scale.

nodes.title: Apply the Scientific Method to Science Itself
nodes.claim: Reforms to scientific institutions (funding mechanisms, review, publication) should be tested experimentally — randomizing scientists across mechanisms, trialing new ones, evaluating retrospectively — rather than adopted on the strength of theory or anecdote. The institutions that demand evidence from researchers rarely apply that standard to themselves.

nodes.title: Approval Uncertainty Deters Investment More Than Approval Cost
nodes.claim: Unpredictability about whether and when a permission will be granted suppresses investment more powerfully than the permission's expected cost or the expected probability of refusal, because investors cannot price or plan around a distribution they cannot estimate. The deterred projects are never applied for, so the damage is invisible in the statistics the system generates about itself.

nodes.title: Approve First, Confirm Later Trades Certainty for Speed and Access
nodes.claim: A conditional approval pathway lets a plausibly effective product reach users before its efficacy is proven, requiring confirmation afterward — trading the certainty that every approved product works for faster and wider access.

nodes.title: Art Progresses by Cumulative Technique
nodes.claim: Art improves the way technology does: techniques and devices accumulate over time, are inherited by later creators, and let them produce work that is more effective at its aims — so later art can be genuinely better, not merely different.

nodes.title: Asset Prices Encode Expectations About the Future
nodes.claim: Asset prices are a real-time, dollar-weighted aggregation of market participants' forward-looking beliefs, so you can read collective expectations about the future — which technologies will matter, which risks loom — out of them.

nodes.title: Attribution Is the Incentive That Sustains Original Work
nodes.claim: Recognition for one's contribution — being credited and valued by peers, more than being paid — is the incentive that motivates people to produce original intellectual work; remove individual attribution and the supply of new work falls.

nodes.title: Automating One Task Barely Dents a Multi-Task Job
nodes.claim: Automating one task of a job that comprises many tasks removes only a small share of the work, so the job — and demand for the worker — largely survives, with time reallocated to the remaining tasks.

nodes.title: Automation Concentrates Where Training Data Is Abundant
nodes.claim: Automated tools cluster around the tasks for which abundant, well-labelled data already exists, leaving data-poor tasks unautomated regardless of their importance.

nodes.title: Automation Substitutes for Scarce Skilled Labor at a Quality Cost
nodes.claim: Automating a task performed by scarce experts trades a small quality decrement for scalability and consistency, expanding access beyond the expert bottleneck.

nodes.title: Background Arts Should Be Unobtrusive Rather Than Maximally Good
nodes.claim: Something experienced peripherally, while attention is on other things, should be judged by how well it serves as a backdrop rather than by how good it is as an object of contemplation. For a backdrop to a wide range of unrelated activities, the right target is politeness and neutrality, not excellence.

nodes.title: Backlash Against Overreach Overshoots Into Status-Quo Lock-In
nodes.claim: Revulsion at a period of destructive overreach can produce procedural defenses that overshoot, shifting the default from building too much to blocking almost everything.

nodes.title: Baumol's Cost Disease Raises the Relative Cost of Unmechanized Work
nodes.claim: When productivity rises in mechanizable sectors, economy-wide wages rise, making activities that genuinely resist mechanization relatively more expensive over time.

nodes.title: Beauty Can Be the Instrument That Achieves a Nonaesthetic Goal
nodes.claim: Attractiveness can be the means to practical ends — better health, higher value, longer life — while ugliness causes neglect and wasteful destruction.

nodes.title: Beauty Is Itself a Function, Not a Rival to Function
nodes.claim: Pleasing the people who use and see a building is one of its purposes, so beauty is a function to be delivered, not a frivolous distraction from function.

nodes.title: Behavior Change Follows Incentives, Not Moral Reasoning
nodes.claim: Large-scale behavior change occurs when self-interest aligns with moral outcomes, not when individuals are persuaded to sacrifice.

nodes.title: Behavior Is the Joint Product of Mind and Environment
nodes.claim: Whether a decision is "rational" cannot be judged from the decision rule alone; the outcome is produced jointly by the cognitive tool and the structure of the environment it operates in -- Herbert Simon's two blades of a scissors. Change the environment and the same rule can shift from optimal to disastrous. (This is the principle of ecological rationality.)

nodes.title: Behavior That Migrates With People Is Cultural, Not Institutional
nodes.claim: When a behavior persists in individuals after they move into a different institutional and legal environment, and is transmitted to their children there, the behavior is carried by internalized culture rather than by the institutions of the place of origin. Portability across contexts is the test that separates the two explanations.

nodes.title: Benchmark Performance Overstates Field Performance
nodes.claim: Scoring well on a curated benchmark systematically overstates how a system will perform in the field, because the benchmark strips out the ambiguity, context, and messiness of real deployment.

nodes.title: Beneficial Competition Has a Sweet Spot Beyond Which It Destroys Value
nodes.claim: Moderate turnover breaks up entrenched arrangements and raises quality, but too-frequent disruption prevents recovery and produces permanent decline; the benefit is hump-shaped in the intensity of competition.

nodes.title: Beneficiary Consent Legitimizes Coercive Change
nodes.claim: A drastic, even coercive change becomes politically durable when those affected are seen to have opted for it themselves, converting what would be imposition into consent.

nodes.title: Binding Constraints Redirect Technological Strategy
nodes.claim: When a technology hits a hard physical limit, progress continues not by pushing the limit but by routing around it — and the chosen workaround reshapes the whole strategy, sometimes trading one constraint for another until a configuration relaxes both.

nodes.title: Binding Price Ceilings Create Shortages and Black Markets
nodes.claim: When a controlled price sits far below the market-clearing level, allocation shifts to queues and illegal side-payments, and the nominal legal protection is effectively lost.

nodes.title: Binding Your Own Hands Defeats Time Inconsistency
nodes.claim: Because rational actors anticipate a policymaker's temptation to renege on an announced plan, the plan is only believed if the policymaker pre-commits — tying its own hands through law or structure so that deviating becomes costly or impossible.

nodes.title: Biological Interventions Can Beat Social Ones on Hard Problems
nodes.claim: For some persistent problems, a biological or medical intervention that requires little behaviour change succeeds where decades of social and behavioural programs failed.

nodes.title: Biotechnology Remains Dependent on Wild Biodiversity
nodes.claim: The tools of synthetic biology are themselves harvested from specific wild organisms, so destroying ecosystems forecloses future discoveries biotech is built on.

nodes.title: Bipartisan Consensus Denies Voters an Exit and Enables Reform
nodes.claim: Contentious reform survives when both major parties commit together, so disaffected voters have no comparable alternative to switch to; the reform lasts only as long as the consensus holds.

nodes.title: Blank-Slate Institutional Design
nodes.claim: Creating new jurisdictions or institutions on greenfield ground, unbound by legacy laws, bureaucracies or rent structures, as a way of obtaining reforms that cannot be passed inside the existing polity.

nodes.title: Blocking Bargains Produces No Development Rather Than Fairer Development
nodes.claim: Where an authority can refuse permission outright but is restricted in what it may demand in exchange for granting it, the effect is not fairer permissions but fewer. Limiting the price of a deal while leaving the veto intact removes the deal, not the veto.

nodes.title: Body Weight Is Defended by a Regulated Setpoint
nodes.claim: Body fatness is not the passive result of willpower and choices; it is actively regulated by the brain around a "setpoint" that the body defends. Attempts to lose weight trigger compensatory responses (more hunger, lower metabolism, stronger food reward) that push weight back up — so dieters fight a homeostatic control system.

nodes.title: Bounded Computation Makes Heuristics Rational
nodes.claim: The mind is a computationally constrained resource, so the optimal decision rule is the best one that is actually feasible to run -- which is usually an approximation or heuristic, not full optimization. Heuristics are rational responses to computational limits, not failures to be rational.

nodes.title: Breaking Entrenched Deals Requires Legitimate Authority
nodes.claim: Long-standing privileges and exemptions can only be overturned by institutions with broadly recognized legitimacy. Personal rulers lack the credibility to revoke inherited bargains; collective institutions can do so, because the revocation is not merely one party defecting.

nodes.title: Bringing an Invention to Market Requires Inventing Its Complements
nodes.claim: A device is only the visible fraction of an invention. Deploying it requires the simultaneous invention of every complementary component the device implies — supply, distribution, measurement, control, and the things it is meant to power — and the scarce skill is foreseeing that whole list before starting, not achieving priority on the device itself.

nodes.title: Bubbles Fund the Future
nodes.claim: Speculative investment over-enthusiasm — "bubbles" — acts as a (costly) mechanism that turns shareholders' money into R&D, capital investment, and infrastructure, building discrete components of the future that outlast the bubble, and coordinating investment toward a shared vision of what's coming.

nodes.title: Build a Simple Parallel System Instead of Reforming the Broken One
nodes.claim: When an existing complex system is broken but cannot be switched off, the way forward is to start a simple working system alongside it rather than to reform it in place, letting the new system grow and eventually supplant the old.

nodes.title: Building Fast Reduces Exposure to Cost-Inflating Shocks
nodes.claim: A shorter construction schedule limits the window in which inflation, external shocks, and political reversals can drive costs up.

nodes.title: Bulk Institutional Procurement Seeds Mass Consumer Familiarity
nodes.claim: Large institutional buyers can acquaint a whole population with a good, seeding the mass consumer demand that outlasts the original contract.

nodes.title: Bundling a Contested Measure Into an Omnibus Bill Provides Political Cover
nodes.claim: Legislators will vote for a controversial policy when it is folded into a larger must-pass package, because they can attribute their vote to other provisions and dodge individual accountability.

nodes.title: Buyers Want Conditional Reasoning, Not Just a Point Probability
nodes.claim: Demand for forecasts is satisfied by analysts who supply contingent scenarios and explanations, a service a bare market price cannot provide, so a market that outputs only a number underserves its would-be customers.

nodes.title: Capable Optimizers Acquire Instrumental Power-Seeking
nodes.claim: For a sufficiently capable agent, seeking power and resisting being shut off are convergent instrumental strategies, because keeping options open and staying operational raise expected utility for almost any final goal.

nodes.title: Capacity Built for Forecast Demand Is Stranded When Demand Falls Short
nodes.claim: Infrastructure sized to a demand forecast becomes stranded, underused capital when the forecast fails to materialize, converting an apparent scale advantage into a liability.

nodes.title: Capacity Is Not Equivalent to Size or Power
nodes.claim: State capacity is distinct from both state size and coercive power. A government can spend heavily, or command a formidable military, and still be unable to execute ordinary administrative tasks competently.

nodes.title: Censorship-Resistance Enables Exit from Authority
nodes.claim: A technology that lets individuals transact or communicate without permission from an intermediary provides an "exit" option from state predation and surveillance — which both empowers dissent and enables illicit use, and constrains what authorities can enforce.

nodes.title: Centralization Reduces Aggregate Externalities
nodes.claim: Replacing many small dispersed sources with one central facility can cut total externalities — pollution, fire risk, insurance cost — even when the central plant is large.

nodes.title: Centralized One-Best-Way Planning Ignores Ground-Level Preferences
nodes.claim: God's-eye schemes that optimise a single abstract order eliminate the variety and individual desires that matter where people actually live.

nodes.title: Centralizing a Decision Converts Local Objections Into National Politics
nodes.claim: Removing an issue from local control means aggrieved residents can express dissent only by swinging their national vote, giving minor parties a defection lever and nationalizing the conflict.

nodes.title: Certainty of Detection Deters More Than Severity of Punishment
nodes.claim: Raising the probability of being caught reduces offending more reliably than raising the penalty, because offenders respond to visible enforcement presence more than to marginal changes in sentence length.

nodes.title: Certification Rigor Scales With the Stakes of Failure
nodes.claim: Downstream users demand testing proportional to the consequences of failure, so the highest-value applications impose the most expensive, time-consuming certification - exactly where a startup is most likely to run out of money.

nodes.title: Cheap Abundance Destroys a Good's Value as a Costly Signal
nodes.claim: When technology makes a formerly scarce good cheap and abundant, it can no longer serve as a credible signal of wealth or sacrifice, collapsing the social equilibrium that rested on its scarcity even if the ritual around it persists.

nodes.title: Cheap Projects Pencil Out on Existing Users Alone
nodes.claim: A low-cost upgrade can be justified by benefits to current users, whereas a high-cost new build needs induced demand — new high-density development — to be viable, and fails if that development never arrives.

nodes.title: Cheap-to-Detect Violations Screen for Hidden Misconduct
nodes.claim: A violation that is easy to detect is worth policing beyond its own harm when it correlates with harder-to-detect wrongdoing: enforcing the cheap signal screens out actors likely to be committing the expensive-to-catch offenses too.

nodes.title: Chicken-and-Egg Between Cost and Application Traps New Technologies
nodes.claim: A material cannot attract the investment to scale without a proven high-value use, but that use cannot be discovered until a cheap version exists to experiment with, trapping the material below the threshold of adoption.

nodes.title: Citation Counts Are a Misleading Proxy for Use
nodes.claim: A method can be in constant practical use while its founding paper accrues few citations, so citation-based indices misclassify workhorses as dormant.

nodes.title: Civil Society Complements State Capacity
nodes.claim: State effectiveness depends not only on bureaucratic capacity but on alignment and cooperation from civil society. Where citizens trust institutions, internalize public goals and coordinate voluntarily, the state achieves more with less coercion.

nodes.title: Co-Locating Discovery and Scaling Under One Roof Speeds Translation
nodes.claim: Institutions that put discovery researchers and production engineers in the same organisation bridge the discovery-to-scale gap, so their decline widens it.

nodes.title: Co-Product Revenue Improves the Economics of a Marginal Extraction
nodes.claim: A primary extraction that is marginal on its own becomes viable when valuable byproducts are harvested from the same process, defraying its cost.

nodes.title: Cognitive Friction in Sources Reduces Their Effective Use
nodes.claim: Compression devices that lower page count - jargon, acronyms, dense paragraphs - shift cognitive load onto readers, and higher reading friction reduces how much a document is actually read and absorbed.

nodes.title: Collective Action & Rent-Seeking
nodes.claim: Collective action failure occurs when policies that are socially harmful persist because benefits are concentrated among a small, organized group while costs are diffuse across a large, uncoordinated population.

nodes.title: Collective Bargaining Extracts Concessions a Lone Actor Cannot
nodes.claim: A coalition bargaining as one can extract privileges, treaty rights, and tax concessions from a powerful counterparty that no individual member could win alone.

nodes.title: Comfort Breeds Risk Aversion
nodes.claim: As people become safer, richer, and more comfortable, they tend to become more risk-averse — they have more to lose and a sharpened instinct to protect it — which can dampen the appetite for the risk-taking that progress requires.

nodes.title: Commissioning Research Can Substitute for Acting
nodes.claim: Launching a research programme is a way of appearing to respond to a problem while deferring any decision about it. Because further study is unobjectionable and open-ended, it functions as a legitimate-looking delay tactic that can hold off action for as long as the study runs.

nodes.title: Communal, Recurring Events Sustain Betting Communities
nodes.claim: Pre-existing fandom and a predictable calendar of interest generate the ongoing participation that keeps a betting market liquid, which one-off niche questions cannot.

nodes.title: Compensating the Losers Unlocks Reform
nodes.claim: A policy that concentrates costs on an identifiable group passes only when some of the revenue it raises is visibly returned to that group, converting would-be blockers into stakeholders.

nodes.title: Compensation Removes the Activation Energy for Latent Altruism
nodes.claim: Payment need not crowd out altruism; it can convert people who want to contribute but are blocked by cost into actual contributors.

nodes.title: Compensatory Overload Becomes a Second Source of Damage
nodes.claim: When surviving units take on extra load to offset an initial injury, the overwork itself progressively degrades them, so decline continues even after the original cause is controlled.

nodes.title: Competing for Uncertain Rewards Wastes Effort Up to the Reward's Value
nodes.claim: When many parties compete for a scarce reward but only some will win, and all must expend effort to compete, total competitive effort is bid up toward the value of the reward itself, dissipating most or all of the gains from having offered it — the same logic as an all-pay auction, where every bidder pays their bid regardless of whether they win.

nodes.title: Competition Selects for Effective Institutions Even When Each Contest Is Destructive
nodes.claim: When many rival units compete under existential stakes, losers exit and winners expand, so the population of survivors improves over time even though each individual contest is costly.

nodes.title: Competitive Differentiation Forces Continual Novelty at the Frontier
nodes.claim: Once a high standard becomes widespread, producers at the top must seek ever more unusual inputs and techniques to stand out, pushing the frontier past imitation into invention.

nodes.title: Competitive Race Dynamics Erode Safety Investment
nodes.claim: When firms or states compete to reach a powerful capability first, especially under winner-takes-all payoffs, each is incentivized to cut safety corners, undermining collective restraint.

nodes.title: Complementary Fixed Infrastructure Caps a Mobile Technology's Growth
nodes.claim: A mobile technology's growth is bounded not by its own engineering but by the fixed land infrastructure it must interface with — ports, bridges, and canals.

nodes.title: Complementary Material Inputs Gate the Diffusion of a General-Purpose Technology
nodes.claim: A general-purpose technology can be invented, demonstrated and commercially proven and still fail to diffuse, because it requires a physical material in quantities the world cannot yet supply. The binding constraint sits in the supply chain rather than in the invention.

nodes.title: Complementary Skills Must Combine in the Same Hands or Community
nodes.claim: Progress stalls when two necessary capabilities sit in separate populations; a bridging group that holds both at once unlocks it.

nodes.title: Completing a Missing Link Activates a Dormant Network
nodes.claim: A small connecting investment that joins the disconnected parts of a large, already-built network can unlock most of that network's latent value, because the expensive bulk of the system already exists.

nodes.title: Complex Order Can Arise from Blind Process Rather Than Design
nodes.claim: Elaborate structure in the natural and social world can be the product of undirected, decentralized processes and chance rather than any central intent or designer.

nodes.title: Complex Systems Kick Back Against Intervention
nodes.claim: A complex system tends to resist and offset changes imposed on it, so interventions provoke compensating reactions that blunt or reverse the intended effect — the system kicks back.

nodes.title: Comprehensive Upzoning Redirects Growth Inward and Lowers Rents
nodes.claim: Broad upzoning not only raises total housing supply but shifts building from the sprawling fringe to central, transit-served land, measurably suppressing rents relative to un-upzoned areas.

nodes.title: Concentrated Upzoning of a Small Area Can Deliver Disproportionate Supply
nodes.claim: Because permitted density enters supply multiplicatively, allowing very high density on a small, well-chosen area can produce more housing than allowing modest increases everywhere — and it does so while touching far fewer people.

nodes.title: Concentrated, Visible Costs Mobilize Opposition More Than Diffuse Benefits
nodes.claim: When a method inflicts visible, localized harm on specific businesses and residents, those concentrated losers mobilize to block it even when the diffuse benefits are larger.

nodes.title: Consent Rules Can Protect the Form of Autonomy While Ignoring Material Welfare
nodes.claim: Institutions can guard informed consent zealously on some questions while never considering participants' real material circumstances, protecting the form of autonomy but not the person's welfare.

nodes.title: Constrain Intent for Capable Actors, Capability for Weak Actors
nodes.claim: Actors with ample resources (states) pursue dangerous capabilities whenever benefits exceed costs, so controlling them means altering incentives and intent; actors without resources (individuals, small groups) are better stopped by denying them the physical means.

nodes.title: Consumable Reagents Trade Material Volume for Energy Cost
nodes.claim: A process can be built either around a reusable agent that must be regenerated, or around a cheap consumable that is used once and discarded. The first pays in energy for every cycle of regeneration; the second pays in the volume of material that must be mined, moved, and processed. Which is cheaper is an empirical question about relative prices, not a matter of elegance.

nodes.title: Context Determines the Aesthetic Experience of a Fixed Object
nodes.claim: The same physical object produces different, genuine aesthetic experiences depending on the category and context through which a viewer perceives it.

nodes.title: Context-Dependent Effects Force Solutions to Be Re-Derived Locally
nodes.claim: Where the effect of an intervention depends on the environment it acts in, a solution validated in one setting does not transfer; it must be rediscovered, re-tuned, or re-validated for each new context. This converts what looks like a one-off research problem into a recurring per-setting cost.

nodes.title: Context-Dependent Rules Cannot Be Enforced Accurately at Scale
nodes.claim: When whether an item violates a rule depends on its surrounding context rather than on anything observable in the item itself, enforcement across very large volumes will generate irreducible false positives and false negatives. Better tools shift the error rate but cannot drive it to zero, because the information needed to make the call is not present in what is being screened.

nodes.title: Controlled Infection Yields More Data Per Person Harmed Than Observing Wild Cases
nodes.claim: Deliberately infecting a few consenting, monitored subjects produces higher-quality, earlier-stage data than studying wild infections, so fewer people must be harmed overall to learn the same thing.

nodes.title: Controlled Production Unlocks Applications the Impure Natural Version Cannot Serve
nodes.claim: The ability to manufacture a material to precise specifications - purity, size, doping - opens entirely new high-value uses that the variable, contaminated natural material was never good enough for, so improving the production process is an upstream enabler of downstream innovation.

nodes.title: Controlling a Biological Trigger Converts a Seasonal Good Into a Year-Round One
nodes.claim: Discovering and controlling the biological trigger for a natural process lets producers schedule output on demand, converting a seasonal good into a year-round, higher-value one.

nodes.title: Controlling a Chokepoint Confers Coercive Leverage
nodes.claim: Whoever controls a chokepoint through which others' essential flows must pass gains coercive leverage over them, because the dependents have little recourse and can be squeezed at will.

nodes.title: Convenience Substitutes Impose a Quality Ceiling
nodes.claim: Shelf-stable, mass-produced convenience inputs win on cost and ease but cap the quality of the final good, limiting the value of even premium complementary goods.

nodes.title: Convention Functions as Decorum, Not Deception
nodes.claim: Presenting a conventional appearance that everyone understands is not the whole literal truth is better modeled as decorum — tact and courtesy toward a shared code — than as deception, because there is no attempt to mislead and no one is actually misled.

nodes.title: Convex Returns to Hours Worked Penalize Time Off
nodes.claim: When pay per hour rises with the number of hours worked, reducing hours costs more than proportionally, so any career interruption is heavily penalised.

nodes.title: Coordinated Boycott Forces a Dependent Counterparty to Concede
nodes.claim: A fully coordinated, enforced withdrawal of trade can force a counterparty dependent on that trade to grant every demand, where scattered individual boycotts fail.

nodes.title: Correctly Assigning Blame Drives Policy Response
nodes.claim: Reform accelerates once the public correctly identifies which decision-maker is responsible for a failure, because accurate attribution creates political pressure that diffuse dissatisfaction does not.

nodes.title: Correlated Failure Raises the Bar for Removing the Human
nodes.claim: Because a single software defect can fail identically across thousands of cases at once, autonomous automation faces a far higher approval bar than a human whose errors are independent and self-limiting.

nodes.title: Corruption Can Be Capacity-Building
nodes.claim: Practices now classified as corruption - selling offices, monopolies and titles, farming out tax collection - can function as capacity-building tools where formal fiscal institutions do not yet exist. They generate revenue without taxation and finance enforcement and administration that would otherwise be unaffordable.

nodes.title: Cost Concentrated in a Removable Input Can Be Cut at the Source
nodes.claim: When most of an intervention's cost and burden sit in one removable input, a redesign that eliminates that input slashes both cost and side effects at once.

nodes.title: Cost-Plus Procurement Inflates Costs
nodes.claim: Procurement contracts that reimburse a supplier's costs plus a guaranteed margin remove the incentive to control costs, predictably producing overruns and delays. Fixed-price commercial contracts, especially under competition, discipline costs by making the supplier bear the overrun.

nodes.title: Costly Ritual Performance Legitimizes an Outcome as Socially Settled
nodes.claim: Enduring a public, rule-governed ordeal — rather than merely asserting a claim — signals sufficient commitment and cost to make the resulting outcome (a marriage, a debt, a status claim) broadly accepted by onlookers as legitimately resolved, converting a private dispute into a socially ratified settlement.

nodes.title: Costs Rise Nonlinearly as a Physical Frontier Is Approached
nodes.claim: Beyond a certain point, pushing a physical process further triggers compounding failures that make each additional increment disproportionately harder and more expensive.

nodes.title: Creative Destruction Applies to Political Units, Not Just Firms
nodes.claim: The Schumpeterian entry-exit-reallocation dynamic operates on states as well as firms: better-governed states enter, worse ones are conquered or overthrown and release their resources, and superior states gain territory.

nodes.title: Credible Private Alternatives Discipline a Monopoly Statistic
nodes.claim: When independent actors can cheaply reproduce or improve on a government metric, the official agency faces pressure to be accurate and transparent or lose public trust to the substitute.

nodes.title: Credible Retaliation Deters More Violence Than It Causes
nodes.claim: A reputation for costly retaliation raises the expected price of a first strike, deterring more violence than the retaliation itself produces and sustaining cooperation.

nodes.title: Credit Conditions Drive Asset Prices More Than Supply
nodes.claim: When credit loosens dramatically, asset prices (especially housing) can be driven far more by borrowing conditions than by the balance of supply and demand — so a price boom coinciding with rising supply is not evidence that supply fails to lower prices.

nodes.title: Credit Expansion Builds or Inflates Depending on Supply Elasticity
nodes.claim: Identical credit expansion produces new construction where supply is elastic and only higher prices where supply is inelastic, so the same monetary impulse has opposite real effects depending on the supply regime.

nodes.title: Creditor Leverage Over a Cash-Strapped Sovereign Buys Policy
nodes.claim: Lending to a sovereign who urgently needs cash converts financial leverage into policy: the creditor extracts privileges, revenue rights, and legal concessions as loan terms.

nodes.title: Crises Reorder Priorities Toward the Future
nodes.claim: Crises cancel some projects and accelerate others, and — by making survival to a future point feel valuable — push individuals and societies to invest in long-term goals. They also can free up slack (time, attention, capital) that gets redirected toward building that future.

nodes.title: Crisis Opens a Window for Long-Blocked Reform
nodes.claim: A repeatedly-rejected proposal advances when an acute failure makes the status quo more costly than the reform, opening a temporary window in which change becomes politically possible.

nodes.title: Cross-Industry Technology Transfer Repurposes an Incumbent's Tools Against Itself
nodes.claim: Techniques, equipment, and skilled personnel developed for one industry can be redeployed to build the industry that displaces it, sharply lowering the entrant's costs.

nodes.title: Crowdsourced Records Extend Measurement Before Official Statistics
nodes.claim: Amateur, user-generated compilations of primary records can measure historical quantities for periods that predate official statistics, provided the sample is validated against the later period where authoritative data does exist and its structural selection biases are explicitly corrected.

nodes.title: Cultural Framing Converts an Imposition Into Local Pride
nodes.claim: Framing an imposed project in a region's own cultural terms can convert it from a resented intrusion into a source of local pride, lowering opposition independent of the project's material effects.

nodes.title: Cultural Pessimism Is a Recurring Constant
nodes.claim: Declarations that culture (art, education, morals) is declining recur in every generation and era; because the complaint is near-universal across time, its presence is weak evidence of actual decline and should lower, not raise, credence in any particular instance.

nodes.title: Culture Enters Through Regulation, Not Consumer Choice
nodes.claim: Where culture shapes the built environment, it usually does so by being codified into regulation, not by expressing itself through unconstrained consumer choice.

nodes.title: Curation Independent of Suppliers Lowers Search Costs in a Vast Option Space
nodes.claim: A neutral, organized collection that neither sells nor brokers reduces the cost of finding relevant options among an overwhelming number, so trusted curation becomes the scarce, valuable good precisely where options are abundant and dispersed.

nodes.title: Cutting Compliance Costs Frees Resources to Buy Local Consent
nodes.claim: Money and management attention spent proving a project's acceptability to a legal process are unavailable for compensating the people who actually bear its costs. Lowering the cost of obtaining permission therefore does not merely make projects cheaper — it reallocates developer resources from compliance toward direct compensation, which is the input that buys genuine local consent.

nodes.title: Deceiving an Agent Requires Modeling Its Mind
nodes.claim: To manipulate an agent, you must represent what that agent perceives, wants, and expects. Deception is therefore a selection pressure for perspective-taking: the deceiver has to run a model of the target's mind and choose the signal that will produce the wrong inference in it. This holds whether the target is a conspecific or another species.

nodes.title: Decentralizing a Judgment Deflects the Legitimacy Cost of Making It
nodes.claim: When an authority's discretionary judgments attract distrust, restructuring the decision so that it emerges from many participants' incentivized actions rather than from the authority's own choice can restore some legitimacy. The gain comes not from better decisions but from a change in attribution: an outcome credited to a process is harder to allege bias in than an outcome credited to a decider.

nodes.title: Decision-Making Scale Shapes Development Outcomes
nodes.claim: The geographic level at which land-use decisions are made determines whether housing gets built. Citywide zoning creates many veto-holding rights and empowers NIMBYs; moving decisions up (state preemption) overwhelms parochial vetoes, while moving them down (block level) lowers the transaction costs of mutually beneficial deals.

nodes.title: Declaring a Problem Solved Dismantles the Capacity to Solve It
nodes.claim: When an institution announces that a problem is solved in principle and that only execution remains, it reallocates its researchers into operations and withdraws the funding that would sustain further discovery. If the announcement turns out to be premature, the capacity needed to respond has already been dismantled.

nodes.title: Declining Research Productivity May Reflect Institutions, Not Exhausted Ideas
nodes.claim: Falling measured research productivity is consistent with two different explanations — ideas are inherently harder to find (the "low-hanging fruit" story), or our institutions for allocating researchers, funding, and locations have gotten worse at finding them — and only the second is within our control; unlike a genuinely finite resource, the stock of "ideas" has never been shown to hit a hard ceiling the way, for instance, oil reserves were long feared to.

nodes.title: Defaults Fail When a Third Party Holds a Veto
nodes.claim: Changing an individual's default choice does little if another actor must still consent and reads the default as an absence of genuine preference.

nodes.title: Defection Is Punished by Exclusion From Club Goods
nodes.claim: A coalition's only enforcement tool is often to revoke a defector's access to the shared privileges it provides, which works only once a formal body exists to coordinate exclusion.

nodes.title: Defense in Depth Beats a Single Countermeasure
nodes.claim: Layering independent measures - prevention, detection, passive containment, and active suppression - reduces catastrophic risk far more than maximizing any one of them, because each layer catches what the others miss.

nodes.title: Delay and Noise in a Chain Amplify Small Shocks
nodes.claim: In a chain of actors who each see only their own link and act with delay, small fluctuations get amplified into large swings up the chain — the bullwhip effect.

nodes.title: Delay Is a Legitimate Market Failure, Not Only Total Absence
nodes.claim: A market can fail by producing the right product far too slowly rather than not at all, so an intervention that merely accelerates an inevitable outcome still creates large value and justifies action.

nodes.title: Delegating State Functions to a Private Monopolist Can Bootstrap Fiscal Capacity
nodes.claim: A state too weak to tax or borrow can escape the trap by granting a single private entity monopoly privileges in exchange for revenue and credit. Protecting one powerful group's property rights is far easier than protecting everyone's, and the arrangement can supply the fiscal base that general capacity is later built on.

nodes.title: Delegating Unpopular Decisions to an Unelected Body Insulates Politicians
nodes.claim: Passing enabling authority while handing the painful specifics - rates, exemptions, thresholds - to an appointed board lets elected officials avoid ownership of the decisions voters resent.

nodes.title: Delegation Is the Default in Low-Capacity States
nodes.claim: When centralized administrative capacity is weak, rulers are forced to delegate core state functions - taxation, policing, adjudication - to local or private actors. Delegation is the normal condition of a low-capacity state rather than a choice it makes.

nodes.title: Deliberate Service Degradation Rations Demand and Diffuses Blame
nodes.claim: An organization facing demand it cannot meet may intentionally degrade its own service so unmet demand disperses to competitors and no accountable executive is singled out for blame.

nodes.title: Deliverable Promises Discipline Politicians Who Can Both Pledge and Build
nodes.claim: When a politician both makes and executes a concrete promise within an electoral term, voters can reward or punish delivery, disciplining the pledge toward feasibility.

nodes.title: Demand Uncertainty Not Technical Impossibility Can Be the Binding Constraint on Innovation
nodes.claim: Some socially valuable products go un-built not because they cannot be made but because would-be inventors doubt anyone will pay, or pay enough, so removing the demand uncertainty can unlock supply that no amount of technical readiness would.

nodes.title: Demand, Not Existence, Determines Whether a Work Is Effectively Available
