nodes.claim: Stylistic originality is a genuine but optional virtue — possessed by a small minority of admired works — not a precondition of legitimacy. Most good buildings (and arguably most good artifacts) repeat received forms, and judging repetition as illegitimate per se mistakes a rare bonus for a baseline requirement.

nodes.title: Outcome-Clarity Determines When to Pick Winners
nodes.claim: Targeted, "pick-a-goal" interventions (Buyers of First Resort, prizes) outperform outcome-blind funding (patents, tax credits) only when the objective is clear and interests few. When society's needs are diffuse and unknowable, outcome-blind mechanisms dominate, because no planner can aggregate all needs the way prices do.

nodes.title: Outsiders Reframe, Insiders Refine
nodes.claim: Scientific progress needs two kinds of work: outsiders, less attached to a field's theories, are better at reframing problems and generating new paradigms; insiders, steeped in the field, are better at refining and applying them.

nodes.title: Overuse Accelerates Resistance in Evolutionary Arms Races
nodes.claim: Deploying a selective agent against a fast-evolving population -- antibiotics against bacteria -- accelerates the very resistance that neutralizes it; misuse (both over- and under-dosing) speeds the arms race, so any such weapon has a usage-dependent shelf life.

nodes.title: Paid Supply Can Coexist With Unpaid Supply Rather Than Crowd It Out
nodes.claim: Introducing compensation for one form of a donated good does not necessarily collapse the adjacent uncompensated supply or degrade its quality.

nodes.title: Parallel Capacity Compresses Schedules
nodes.claim: Deploying many units of construction capacity at once, working continuously, converts a long serial schedule into a short parallel one.

nodes.title: Parallel Independent Bets Need Only One Winner
nodes.claim: When several independent approaches target the same breakthrough, the field's success depends on any one of them working, not on all of them, so diversity of attempts lowers the overall risk of failure.

nodes.title: Parking Mandates Dictate Building Typology
nodes.claim: Minimum-parking requirements dictate a building's basic form, and changes in those minimums drive shifts between whole building typologies.

nodes.title: Participatory Veto Points Empower Small Groups Over Majorities
nodes.claim: Public-participation procedures create veto points that a small, motivated minority can use to override both democratic majorities and market signals.

nodes.title: Paying for Outputs Beats Paying for Inputs When Funders Cannot Pick Winners
nodes.claim: Where a funder cannot tell in advance which approach or which team will succeed, committing to reward a defined result outperforms funding chosen inputs, because it transfers selection to the people with the information and pays only on delivery.

nodes.title: Peer Review Is Gatekeeping, Not Quality Control
nodes.claim: Peer review largely functions as opaque gatekeeping — deciding what gets published via the idiosyncratic, private judgments of available reviewers — rather than as reliable quality control that catches errors or flawed methods.

nodes.title: People-Not-Projects Funding Outperforms Deliverable-Monitored Grants
nodes.claim: Funding researchers with long time horizons, minimal reporting requirements, and no fixed deliverables produces more innovative output than funding narrowly-scoped projects under continuous milestone monitoring, because monitoring pressures researchers to chase a publishable confirmation of their original plan rather than follow up promising surprises that emerge along the way.

nodes.title: Per Capita Growth Can Come from the Denominator, Not the Numerator
nodes.claim: Income per capita is total income divided by population, so living standards can be raised either by increasing output or by restraining population growth. Limiting the denominator is a genuine and historically demonstrated development path, an alternative to industrializing the numerator rather than a consolation prize.

nodes.title: Percentage Gains Are Uninterpretable Without the Baseline
nodes.claim: A reported proportional improvement conveys almost no information about absolute value unless the starting level is stated, and improvements are systematically easier to achieve — and therefore preferentially reported — where the baseline is low.

nodes.title: Perishability Plus Slow Transport Confines a Good to Local Production
nodes.claim: A perishable good that cannot survive the transit time to distant markets must be produced locally, however expensively, until transport or preservation improves.

nodes.title: Permissions Translate Into Building
nodes.claim: Granting more planning permissions does lead to more homes actually being built (with a lag) — contradicting the "land banking" claim that developers hoard permissions and drip-feed supply to keep prices high. A less-than-1:1 permission-to-build ratio is not evidence that permissions are useless.

nodes.title: Physical, Economic, and Legal Frontiers Diverge as Technology Matures
nodes.claim: As a technology matures, three ceilings on its use separate: first the physical limit (what's engineerable), then the economic limit (what's profitable, usually well below physical), and finally the legal limit (what's permitted), which arises to cap externalities once the economic frontier has risen enough to make them salient.

nodes.title: Placing an Input Where It Persists Multiplies Its Effect
nodes.claim: Delivering the same input where it lasts longer and spreads further multiplies its effect per unit, so location and residence time, not just quantity, determine impact.

nodes.title: Placing the Cost of a Restriction on Those Who Demand It Disciplines Demand for It
nodes.claim: When the people who impose a restriction also bear its cost, they demand far less of it. Regulation is over-supplied wherever its benefits are concentrated on those who choose it and its costs fall on others; making the chooser pay converts an unlimited demand into a priced choice.

nodes.title: Platform R&D Before a Crisis Shortens Response Time
nodes.claim: Investing in transferable, family-level scientific groundwork before an emergency means the response starts from an advanced base rather than from scratch, compressing the time to a working countermeasure.

nodes.title: Policy Experimentation via Jurisdictional Autonomy
nodes.claim: Delegating authority to sub-national units so they can experiment with policy and institutional design.

nodes.title: Political and Disruption Costs Can Retire a Cheaper Technology
nodes.claim: A technology superior on dollar cost gets abandoned when its non-monetary externalities — disruption, harm, opposition — become socially intolerable, even if the replacement is more expensive.

nodes.title: Politics Is Downstream of Technological Change
nodes.claim: The material conditions created by technological and scientific breakthroughs determine and constrain the forms that politics, culture, and consciousness can take; political events are largely effects of prior changes in lived experience, not the primary causes of historical change.

nodes.title: Pollution Rises Then Falls As Incomes Rise
nodes.claim: For many local pollutants, emissions per capita rise during early industrialization and then fall past a threshold income — the environmental Kuznets curve. The turning point is not automatic: it reflects that citizens demand clean air once basic needs are met, and that richer states can afford abatement technology and enforce it.

nodes.title: Pooling Fragmented Plots Enables Coordinated Redevelopment
nodes.claim: Legally merging many small landholdings into one collective parcel, redrawing the boundaries to carve out space for infrastructure, and redistributing the remainder lets a city achieve replanning and density that fragmented ownership otherwise makes impossible.

nodes.title: Pooling Heterogeneous Subgroups Hides the Conditional Result
nodes.claim: A headline average over a mixed population can hide the true result for a well-defined subgroup, misleading anyone who does not condition on the relevant variables.

nodes.title: Pooling Individual Records Into a Central Dataset Creates Collective Value
nodes.claim: Aggregating many individuals' private records into a shared dataset produces analytical value none could obtain alone, while still returning private benefit to each contributor.

nodes.title: Poorly Drafted Legislation Is Redefined by Litigation, Not Legislators
nodes.claim: Every ambiguity in a hurried statute becomes a court case, so opponents can gut a law through litigation without ever repealing it.

nodes.title: Population Scale Guarantees a Resistance Mutation
nodes.claim: When an intervention is applied to an enormous population, the sheer number of individuals makes a rare escape mutation near-certain to arise, and selection then favours the resistant variant, blunting the intervention over time.

nodes.title: Population Size Determines Military and Geopolitical Power
nodes.claim: In the pre-industrial and early-industrial world a state's ability to project force was set primarily by the number of people it could feed and conscript, so relative population is the best single predictor of relative great-power standing. A country whose population stops growing loses its position even while performing well internally.

nodes.title: Population Size Drives Idea Production
nodes.claim: Because ideas are non-rivalrous — one good idea can benefit everyone at once — a larger population tends to produce more ideas and faster progress. Fewer people means fewer new ideas, so demographic decline is a drag on innovation in the long run.

nodes.title: Portability Gates a Technology's Real-World Use
nodes.claim: A technology's practical usefulness can be capped by the portability of its hardware rather than by its demonstrated capability: a system that works only tethered to lab equipment changes little in daily life, however impressive in the lab.

nodes.title: Positive Externalities Are Systematically Undersupplied
nodes.claim: When the benefits of an effort accrue to the whole system rather than to its producer, the producer underinvests in it relative to the social optimum.

nodes.title: Positive-Results Bias Distorts Science
nodes.claim: Because journals, funders, and audiences reward exciting positive findings over null ones, the scientific record fills with false positives: results that are statistical flukes, p-hacked, or confined to safe incremental questions where a positive answer was nearly guaranteed.

nodes.title: Practice Precedes Theory in Institutional Innovation
nodes.claim: A workable institution can emerge from political improvisation and only later be rationalised by academic theory, rather than being derived from theory and then implemented.

nodes.title: Pre-Harm Enforcement Is More Politically Feasible Than Post-Harm Punishment
nodes.claim: Moderate sanctions applied before harm occurs - fines, license bans for exceeding a threshold - are more readily accepted by courts and the public than harsh penalties imposed after a rare catastrophic outcome.

nodes.title: Pre-registration Curbs P-Hacking
nodes.claim: Requiring researchers to declare their hypotheses and analysis methods before they collect data removes the freedom to selectively choose methods and subgroups that yield a desired result, sharply reducing false positives.

nodes.title: Precision Lets Physical Objects Conform to Mathematical Idealizations
nodes.claim: Mechanization becomes possible only when manufacturing tolerances tighten enough that real parts behave like their idealized designs, reducing the friction and variation that defeat a design on paper.

nodes.title: Prescriptive Standards Ban Novel Methods by Specifying the Old One
nodes.claim: When regulation specifies the method, materials, and measurements rather than the performance to be achieved, any technology that reaches the same result by a different route is non-compliant by construction — not because it was judged and rejected, but because the rulebook encodes the incumbent's recipe as the definition of adequacy.

nodes.title: Preservation Technology Detaches Consumption From Harvest Location and Time
nodes.claim: Canning and refrigeration sever the link between where and when a perishable is produced and where and when it is consumed, opening distant year-round markets.

nodes.title: Prestige Allocates Talent and Attention
nodes.claim: Where talent and attention flow is governed by prestige and glory, not money alone. Visible, awe-inspiring projects attract disproportionate talent, acclaim, and inspiration, while equally valuable but unglamorous work is neglected.

nodes.title: Prestige Demand Subsidizes the Innovation That Later Democratizes a Good
nodes.claim: Seemingly frivolous luxury spending funds the technical and commercial innovation that eventually makes a good cheap and widely available.

nodes.title: Prestige Design Imposes Cost Without User Benefit
nodes.claim: Bespoke, award-seeking design adds large cost that serves architects' and clients' status rather than the users of the facility.

nodes.title: Prestige-Based Credit Degrades Communication Quality
nodes.claim: When academic reward tracks the prestige of the publication venue rather than whether work is read and understood, authors optimize for gatekeeper approval over reader comprehension, so communication quality erodes.

nodes.title: Preventing Nominal Defaults Can Require Sacrificing Other Actors
nodes.claim: Averting a cascade of nominal defaults is achieved by shifting the loss onto other parties - inflating away debt, bailing out one sector while letting another fail - rather than by making anyone whole.

nodes.title: Prevention Investment Is Cheap Relative to the Catastrophe It Averts
nodes.claim: The cost of standing protective infrastructure looks large in isolation but is small relative to the catastrophe it prevents, making continuous investment rational even when no disaster is currently visible.

nodes.title: Price Caps Below Cost Are Paid in Quality, Not Price
nodes.claim: When a regulator caps the price of a good below its cost of production but cannot equally regulate its quality, the provider satisfies the cap by cutting the unregulated dimension — so the good becomes cheap and bad rather than cheap and good, and the shortfall is paid by users in unreliability instead of money.

nodes.title: Price Controls Degrade the Quality of the Controlled Good
nodes.claim: Capping the price of a good below market removes the provider's incentive to maintain and invest in it, so the stock of the controlled good deteriorates over time.

nodes.title: Price Controls Shrink the Supply of the Controlled Good
nodes.claim: A binding price ceiling pushes units out of the controlled market - into ownership, short-term rental, or conversion - reducing the stock available to the very people the control was meant to help.

nodes.title: Priced Access Is Progressive When the Priced Good Is Consumed by the Rich
nodes.claim: A flat fee is not regressive if the taxed activity is undertaken disproportionately by the wealthy, because the burden then falls mostly on high-income users despite the uniform price.

nodes.title: Prices Reveal Preferences That Quantities Conceal
nodes.claim: Letting participants bid reveals their true relative valuations, information that a central planner allocating fixed quantities can never observe.

nodes.title: Private Self-Provision Substitutes for Failed Public Infrastructure at Higher Cost
nodes.claim: When a shared public system fails to deliver reliably, users do not go without — they duplicate it privately at individual scale, and because the private substitute forgoes every economy of scale and load-diversity advantage of the shared system, society pays far more in total for a worse product.

nodes.title: Prizes Reward Disclosure of Existing Solutions, Not Novel Invention
nodes.claim: The most historically effective "innovation prizes" did not elicit genuinely novel ideas from nowhere; they paid inventors to disclose and develop solutions whose theoretical basis already existed but had been kept secret, unpublished, or merely unimplemented for lack of funding.

nodes.title: Procedural Review Laws Give Opponents Veto Leverage
nodes.claim: Environmental-disclosure and process statutes let affected parties block projects on procedural grounds — inadequate impact disclosure — not just on substance, empowering opposition to disruptive methods.

nodes.title: Process Cost and Substantive Stringency Are Separable
nodes.claim: The burden a regulatory regime imposes decomposes into the cost of navigating the process (delay, paperwork, unpredictability) and the cost of complying with the substantive standard (the actual mitigations required). These are causally independent: a regime can be made faster, cheaper, and more predictable while holding the standard constant or raising it. Treating regulatory burden as a single dial that trades off against protection is a category error.

nodes.title: Process Innovation in Extraction Rivals Product Invention in Consequence
nodes.claim: Changing how a material is won from the earth can matter as much to the course of a technological era as inventing the devices that use it - and yet extraction innovators are systematically forgotten, because the history of technology is written about artefacts rather than about inputs.

nodes.title: Procurement Incentives Shape What Gets Delivered
nodes.claim: The terms of a public contract determine what actually gets delivered: pay suppliers for an activity and you get more of that activity, not the outcome you wanted. Aligning payment with the desired result — and publishing performance metrics — is as important as the budget.

nodes.title: Profit From an Edge Scales With Market Size, Not Just Accuracy
nodes.claim: The money an informed trader can make is the product of the edge and the volume they can transact, so a small edge on a large market beats a large edge on a thin one.

nodes.title: Proportionate Regulatory Review Scales Scrutiny to Actual Risk
nodes.claim: Review effort should track the real incremental risk of a project; abbreviating review for low-risk, already-developed sites avoids paying for scrutiny that buys no safety.

nodes.title: Proven Technology Avoids the Testing Tax of Innovation
nodes.claim: Choosing mature, proven technology over the cutting edge avoids the long testing, debugging, and delay that novel systems require.

nodes.title: Proving a Safe Threshold Requires Proving a Negative
nodes.claim: A no-threshold precautionary rule perpetuates itself because overturning it means demonstrating that no effect exists below some dose — proving a negative — which evidence can never do conclusively, biasing the status quo in the rule's favour.

nodes.title: Proving Prevention Requires Deliberate Exposure
nodes.claim: Demonstrating that a preventive measure works requires deliberately exposing protected subjects to the threat, since without a challenge the absence of disease is indistinguishable from chance.

nodes.title: Proximate vs Ultimate Causes in Mental Disorder
nodes.claim: Identifying the neural or genetic correlates of a disorder does not explain why the disorder exists. Proximate causes describe how a trait operates; ultimate causes explain why it evolved or persists, and a research programme that pursues only the first can accumulate detail without gaining understanding.

nodes.title: Psychiatry Lacks a Coherent Theory of Disorder
nodes.claim: Psychiatry has struggled to make cumulative progress because it lacks an agreed-upon, principled definition of what constitutes mental disorder.

nodes.title: Public Arts Impose Their Costs on Non-Choosers
nodes.claim: Where a work is experienced involuntarily by people who did not commission or choose it, the maker's aesthetic preferences become an externality. The relevant question stops being whether the work is good and becomes who bears the cost of it being disliked.

nodes.title: Public Legal Codes Displace Privately-Negotiated Order
nodes.claim: When a public legal code offers all merchants reliable adjudication, it displaces the privately-negotiated self-governance a coalition provided, removing its reason to exist.

nodes.title: Public Risk-Bearing Enables Private Risk-Taking
nodes.claim: Governments (and some mission-driven private actors) can absorb risks that private buyers cannot — guaranteeing demand, indemnifying failure, funding by milestone — which unlocks ambitious private development that would otherwise be too risky to attempt, especially for startups.

nodes.title: Public, Continuous Review Outpaces Journal Gatekeeping
nodes.claim: When research circulates openly -- as preprints, forum threads, shared code and data -- review becomes a continuous, distributed, public process that corrects and contextualizes work far faster than the closed, pre-publication gatekeeping of journals.

nodes.title: Public-Private Data-Sharing Substitutes for Infeasible Central Testing
nodes.claim: When a central authority cannot itself test every unit, it can make producers partners — trading published analyses for their raw records — to build a dataset neither could produce alone.

nodes.title: Publish-or-Perish Rewards Volume Over Rigor
nodes.claim: Academic career rewards (tenure, promotion, prestige) attach to publication count and journal impact, so the system incentivizes producing many papers rather than fewer rigorous ones — generating a chronic oversupply of low-quality, often redundant research.

nodes.title: Published Knowledge Can Remain Latent Until Retrieved
nodes.claim: Valuable findings can exist in the literature yet stay effectively unknown because no one connects them to the problems they solve; progress is partly a retrieval problem, not only a discovery problem. A latent finding awakens only when its surrounding environment — tools, theory, or an adjacent field — becomes receptive.

nodes.title: Punishing Rule-Breaking Chills the Discretion Systems Depend On
nodes.claim: Aggressive punishment for procedural deviation suppresses not just abuse but the frontline judgment, waste-avoidance, and improvisation that would advance the system's own goals, because agents rationally refuse to gamble their careers.

nodes.title: Punishment Severity Is Capped by Perceived Proportionality
nodes.claim: When a sanction exceeds what a community judges fitting for an act, jurors nullify, victims withhold cooperation, and enforcers hesitate, so disproportionate penalties become self-defeating rather than more deterrent.

nodes.title: Quality Adjustment Separates True Price Change From Getting More for Your Money
nodes.claim: When a good improves along measurable dimensions, part of its price rise buys a better product and should not be counted as inflation; netting this out via quality adjustment is essential or the index overstates price growth.

nodes.title: r minus g Determines Debt Sustainability
nodes.claim: The burden and sustainability of public debt are governed not by its level but by the gap between the real interest rate paid on it (r) and the economy's growth rate (g). When r − g is negative, the debt-to-GDP ratio decays exponentially without any repayment; when positive, it compounds and requires tax rises or spending cuts.

nodes.title: Random Assignment Reveals Causal Effects That Correlations Miss
nodes.claim: Randomly assigning who receives an intervention makes treatment and control groups comparable, so outcome differences can be attributed causally to the intervention; relationships seen in observational data frequently weaken or reverse under this test because they conflate treatment with selection.

nodes.title: Randomized Broad Damage Forecloses Adaptive Resistance
nodes.claim: An intervention that damages a target's machinery broadly and at random leaves no single pathway for the target to adapt around, so resistance cannot evolve — unlike a precise intervention that selects for escape mutants.

nodes.title: Ratcheting Commitments Beat One-Shot Targets
nodes.claim: Hard collective problems are better solved by an agreement that tightens its commitments over time as evidence and capability grow than by a single fixed target set up front — which is typically both too weak and politically frozen.

nodes.title: Rationality Is Error-Minimization, Not Bias-Elimination
nodes.claim: The goal of a good decision rule is to minimize total error, not to eliminate bias; since error decomposes into bias plus variance, a deliberately biased rule can be the rational choice when it lowers overall error.

nodes.title: Rationed Demand Rebounds Explosively When the Constraint Is Lifted
nodes.claim: Demand held back by rationing accumulates and floods the market at once when the constraint is removed, overwhelming fixed supply and producing a sharp price spike.

nodes.title: Rationing Substitutes for Price When Prices Are Held Below Market
nodes.claim: Holding an interest rate or output price below its market-clearing level produces allocation by queue and quota rather than by price, because something must ration the resulting excess demand.

nodes.title: Reaction Rate Is Set by Surface Area, Not Total Mass
nodes.claim: For processes that occur at an interface, throughput scales with exposed surface area rather than with the bulk quantity present. A geologically slow process can therefore be accelerated by orders of magnitude purely by subdividing the material, without changing the chemistry at all.

nodes.title: Realized Progress Reveals New Flaws That Fuel the Next Advance
nodes.claim: Because nothing is perfect and standards themselves rise as we improve, each realised advance exposes new dissatisfactions that drive the next round of improvement.

nodes.title: Reciprocity Is More Palatable Than Cash for Contested Goods
nodes.claim: For goods people resist commodifying, giving contributors a claim on the same system's output raises supply while avoiding the moral backlash a price tag triggers.

nodes.title: Recombining Distant Findings Unlocks Latent Discovery
nodes.claim: Breakthroughs often come from connecting a result in one field with tools or facts in another, so bridging disciplinary distance releases knowledge already present in the literature.

nodes.title: Records Advance Fastest Where Permission Is Weakest
nodes.claim: Frontier records — tallest, largest, cheapest — advance fastest in exactly those domains and places where permission and regulation are weakest.

nodes.title: Recycling the Payments Reconciles Market Efficiency With Equitable Distribution
nodes.claim: Redistributing the proceeds of a market back to participants by need lets a price mechanism capture efficiency gains while preserving equitable distribution, so the two need not trade off.

nodes.title: Red Teaming Counteracts Consensus Capture
nodes.claim: Institutionalizing an adversarial role — people explicitly tasked and funded to attack, refute, and replicate prevailing claims — counteracts groupthink in a way that voluntary individual skepticism cannot, because it removes the social penalty for dissent by making dissent the assigned job.

nodes.title: Redefining What Counts as Ore Expands Reserves Without New Discovery
nodes.claim: A mineral reserve is an economic category, not a geological one: it is the material that can be extracted profitably at current costs and prices. A fall in extraction cost therefore creates reserves out of rock that was previously worthless, without anyone finding anything new.

nodes.title: Reducing a Product to a Reusable Primitive Multiplies Its Applications
nodes.claim: Treating a substance as a decomposable set of standard building blocks, rather than a single finished good, lets one input be recombined into unrelated product categories.

nodes.title: Reform Is Easiest Where There Is No Incumbent Constituency
nodes.claim: The political cost of a change is determined by how many identifiable people already occupy the ground it affects. Directing reform at sites, sectors, or populations with no resident constituency lets a government achieve at low cost what would be impossible against an organized incumbent.

nodes.title: Reform Sticks When It Makes the Losers Better Off Too
nodes.claim: Institutional change survives opposition when it is engineered so that even incumbents and potential losers gain, converting adversaries into acquiescent or active supporters rather than requiring their defeat.

nodes.title: Reformers Without a Constituency Cannot Sustain Political Change
nodes.claim: A reformer who depends solely on a patron, lacking a party or organized base, can win concessions but is defeated once the patron's incentive to back reform fades.

nodes.title: Reframing Around User Need Redirects Innovation Trajectories
nodes.claim: Treating a material's design problem as defined by the end user's body or task — rather than by the substance's inherent properties — reorients R&D toward previously unconsidered performance dimensions (moisture transport, thermal regulation, weight) and can rescue a technology that had been written off under the old framing.

nodes.title: Regulating by Origin Rather Than Properties Detaches Scrutiny from Risk
nodes.claim: When a regulatory regime classifies a product by the process that produced it rather than by the properties it actually has, the intensity of scrutiny stops tracking the hazard. Two physically indistinguishable products receive wildly different treatment, and two products with the same label can carry very different risks.

nodes.title: Regulation Inherited From an Analogous Industry Imposes Irrelevant Costs
nodes.claim: When no tailored rules exist, a new technology defaults to a neighboring industry's regulatory regime and incurs compliance costs for risks it does not actually carry.

nodes.title: Regulation, Not Culture, Determines Built Form
nodes.claim: Cross-national differences in urban form usually attributed to deep cultural preferences are overwhelmingly produced by building codes and zoning rules, not by buyers, architects, or heritage.

nodes.title: Regulator Unfamiliarity Raises the Cost of Approval
nodes.claim: When a regulator lacks experience with a domain, it cannot easily judge whether a result is normal or alarming, so evaluation becomes slow, uncertain, and expensive — deterring applications even for sound products.

nodes.title: Regulators Are Blamed for Visible Harms but Not for Forgone Benefits
nodes.claim: A regulator's personal and institutional costs are asymmetric: an approval that causes a visible harm is attributed to them, while a refusal that forgoes a large benefit is attributed to nobody. Rational regulators therefore over-refuse, and the resulting losses never appear in any account of the agency's performance.

nodes.title: Regulatory and Safety Requirements Trade Off Against Innovation
nodes.claim: Rigorous certification born of past disasters increases safety but raises the cost and uncertainty of pursuing new materials and methods, deterring the up-front investment that innovation requires.

nodes.title: Regulatory Limits Become Optimization Targets
nodes.claim: When a legal threshold caps what would otherwise be economical, activity bunches right at the limit and design is contorted to hug it — the rule becomes the thing everyone optimizes toward, often producing distinctive artifacts that exist only because of the code.

nodes.title: Regulatory Lock-In Preserves an Obsolete Technology
nodes.claim: Once a method is written into an approval standard, the incumbent persists long after a superior substitute is validated, because switching means re-clearing regulatory hurdles nobody is paid to clear.

nodes.title: Regulatory Safety Mandates Can Surface Unintended Benefits
nodes.claim: Requiring a drug to be tested for harms across broader endpoints or populations than its original indication can reveal large unanticipated benefits it was never designed to demonstrate.

nodes.title: Reinforcement Learning from Self-Play Beats Human-Knowledge Engineering
nodes.claim: When a system trains by trial-and-error against itself rather than ingesting human-curated domain knowledge and heuristics, it can surpass systems built on hand-coded expertise, and even discover strategies humans never found.

nodes.title: Relational Capacity Runs Out Faster in Tighter Space
nodes.claim: How long an informal host can shelter someone depends on the physical room available: a spare bedroom lasts far longer than a shared living space before tolerance is exhausted.

nodes.title: Relative Decline Can Occur Without Absolute Failure
nodes.claim: An economy (or institution) can fall behind a rising rival while still performing about as well as its own resources and technology allow; "decline" measured relative to a faster grower is often mistaken for absolute failure or self-inflicted error.

nodes.title: Relative Misery Drives Suicide
nodes.claim: Suicide risk may track relative rather than absolute misery: being sad while those around you are happy is more dangerous than being sad in a generally unhappy time, because others' contentment sharpens the sense of not belonging.

nodes.title: Relaxing a Deadline Constraint Enables Sequencing Rather Than Sacrifice
nodes.claim: Extending a hard deadline converts a forced simultaneous trade-off into a sequential one, letting a person do both activities in turn instead of sacrificing one.

nodes.title: Relieving One Bottleneck Shifts It Downstream
nodes.claim: Solving the binding constraint in a process does not end scarcity; it moves the bottleneck to the next step, which then becomes the limiting cost.

nodes.title: Removing a Distance Constraint Nationalizes a Local Advantage
nodes.claim: Eliminating a transport or storage barrier lets a locally superior resource benefit distant users, turning a local edge into a national one.

nodes.title: Removing a Tax on an Input Lowers the Final Good's Cost
nodes.claim: Repealing a tax on an intermediate input lowers the cost of everything built from it, sometimes unlocking whole downstream industries.

nodes.title: Removing an In-Place Hazard Can Create More Exposure Than Leaving It
nodes.claim: When a hazard is dangerous only once disturbed, proactively removing it wherever it exists can release more of the harmful agent than leaving it undisturbed would.

nodes.title: Removing an Item From Its Category Label Enables Cross-Application Discovery
nodes.claim: Presenting objects stripped of their marketed use-category lets users re-imagine them for purposes the original classification would have foreclosed, so deliberately withholding the intended-use frame expands the space of discovered applications.

nodes.title: Removing Disincentives Beats Adding Persuasion
nodes.claim: When participation carries large uncompensated private costs, neutralizing those costs raises supply far more than exhortation or default-setting does.

nodes.title: Removing Mortality Risk Is a Stronger Incentive Than Subsidizing the Activity
nodes.claim: When an activity carries a meaningful chance of death, eliminating that risk changes behaviour more than any comparable reduction in its monetary or time cost. A risk of losing one's life is not tradeable against convenience, so removing it relaxes a constraint rather than merely improving a price.

nodes.title: Removing One Node Can Cascade Through an Ecological Network
nodes.claim: Eliminating a species can trigger unanticipated knock-on effects through the web of predator-prey and competitive relationships it sits in, so a deliberate extinction carries hard-to-predict second-order risks.

nodes.title: Repair Capacity Makes Dose Rate Matter, Not Just Total Dose
nodes.claim: Because a living system repairs damage over time, many small doses spread out are less harmful than one large dose of the same total — contradicting any model that assumes harm simply accumulates.

nodes.title: Repeatable Design Requires a Predictable Approval Regime
nodes.claim: Building a fleet of identical units — the precondition for learning-by-doing and falling unit costs in capital-intensive infrastructure — is only possible where the approval regime is consistent enough that the same design can be permitted repeatedly. Case-by-case discretion forces each project to be redesigned for its own consent, destroying the repetition on which cost declines depend.

nodes.title: Replication Across Sites Separates Genetics From Environment
nodes.claim: Observing the same unit's performance across many independent sites disentangles its intrinsic quality from local conditions and management.

nodes.title: Replication Failure Can Reflect Unreported Conditions Rather Than a False Finding
nodes.claim: When other laboratories cannot reproduce a result, the most common explanation is not that the original finding was wrong but that some condition necessary to it went unrecorded, because the original workers did not know it mattered. The finding is real and the protocol is incomplete.

nodes.title: Representative Institutions Trade Ruler Constraint for Fiscal Capacity
nodes.claim: Parliaments let rulers credibly commit to property rights and constraints in exchange for tax revenue, improving governance and growth.

nodes.title: Research Faces an Irreducible Risk–Reward Tradeoff
nodes.claim: As in finance, research offers no low-risk, high-reward options: high-reward projects are inherently more likely to fail. Funding systems that demand both high impact and near-certain success are demanding the impossible, and get incremental or misrepresented work instead.

nodes.title: Research Neglect Reflects Who Does the Research
nodes.claim: What science studies and funds reflects who does the science: fields relevant to under-represented groups are systematically under-researched and under-funded, because researchers, investors, and rule-makers are disproportionately drawn from other groups and less attuned (or more uncomfortable) with those problems.

nodes.title: Restricting Development Lowers Property Value Unless Externalities Are Large
nodes.claim: Prohibiting development on a parcel destroys the option to develop it, and an asset that cannot be built on is worth less than one that can. Restriction only raises value where the amenity gained from restricting the neighbours exceeds the option value lost on one's own land - and in the most expensive cities it does not come close.

nodes.title: Revealed Preference Across Market Segments Discriminates Between Rival Explanations
nodes.claim: Comparing where a good persists across price tiers - budget versus elite segments - discriminates between a cost-based and a taste-based explanation for its decline.

nodes.title: Revealed Preference Reveals Quality
nodes.claim: When superior past options are available at trivial cost and people still choose something else, that choice is evidence the chosen thing is better for them — revealed preference is a more reliable quality signal than expert pronouncement.

nodes.title: Revenue Concentrated in a Single Seizable Base Invites Capture
nodes.claim: A state that draws most of its revenue from one physically concentrated, easily seized source is unusually fragile. Any rival who takes that source simultaneously funds himself and defunds the centre, which makes rebellion cheap and turns the revenue base itself into the primary military objective.

nodes.title: Reviewer Agreement Is Low Enough to Be Near-Random
nodes.claim: With only one to three reviewers per paper, inter-reviewer agreement is so low that a paper's accept/reject outcome is closer to a coin flip than a reliable signal of quality -- the reviews reflect neither a real consensus nor a designed diversity, but chance.

nodes.title: Revival Movements Mature From Recreation Into Original Creation
nodes.claim: Movements that begin by recovering a lost past accumulate the skills, inputs, and demanding audience that eventually enable forward-looking creation beyond anything historical.

nodes.title: Reviving a Natural Material Can Recreate Import Dependence
nodes.claim: Scaling demand for a naturally sourced input concentrated in one country reproduces the same strategic dependence that afflicts advanced synthetics.

nodes.title: Rewarding Throughput Over Value Produces Waste
nodes.claim: A system that rewards moving volume rather than delivering value drives waste, because participants optimise the measured quantity even when it destroys usefulness.

nodes.title: Rigorous Evidence De-Risks Deviation from the Status Quo
nodes.claim: Because institutional risk-takers capture little upside but bear the reputational downside of failure, unconventional ideas stall; value-neutral experimental evidence lowers the personal and political cost of deviating and can legitimize ideas once dismissed as crazy.

nodes.title: Rising Intolerance for Disruption Raises a Method's Effective Cost
nodes.claim: As public tolerance for construction nuisance falls, the political price of a disruptive method climbs independent of its engineering cost, shifting the chosen technology.

nodes.title: Rising Wealth Can Substitute for Changing Values
nodes.claim: Making people richer changes what they value, so material progress can accomplish the same ends that moral persuasion aims at. In the existential-risk case, wealth makes people value life more (effectively lowering their discount rate on survival), so alleviating poverty can be a more effective route to safety than either direct safety spending or arguing people into caring about the long run.

nodes.title: Risk Regulation Tracks Attributability, Not Magnitude
nodes.claim: How heavily a hazard is regulated depends on whether its victims can be individually identified and traced back to a cause, not on how many people it kills. A hazard that kills a great many people diffusely is tolerated; one that kills a few people identifiably is banned.

nodes.title: Ritualized Contests Channel Conflict Into Bounded, Non-Escalatory Violence
nodes.claim: Societies facing chronic risk of lethal dispute — where every adult is armed and no court system exists — develop rule-bound contests (duels) that let aggression be expressed and disputes resolved within limits most participants survive, substituting for open-ended, potentially indefinitely escalating violence such as feuds, revenge cycles, or unregulated warfare.

nodes.title: Room-Temperature Biostabilization Collapses Distribution Infrastructure
nodes.claim: A carrier that preserves a fragile biomolecule at ambient temperature eliminates the cold chain, dissolving the entire logistical network a product previously required.

nodes.title: Routine Administrative Correction Beats Discretionary Political Override
nodes.claim: A system that continuously corrects local shortfalls through ordinary, low-drama administrative duty outperforms one that relies on occasional high-profile political intervention, because the override attracts opposition each time it is used while the routine duty does not.

nodes.title: Salience-Raising Messaging Can Backfire by Normalizing the Target Behavior
nodes.claim: Awareness campaigns that make an offence more mentally available can make it seem more common, and therefore more normal, undercutting the deterrent they intend.

nodes.title: Salient Evidence Mobilizes Action
nodes.claim: Vivid, legible evidence — a striking image, a concrete number — mobilizes political and public action far more powerfully than abstract models, even when the models carried the same information earlier.

nodes.title: Salient Gains Beat Diffuse Pain in Selling a Policy
nodes.claim: A reform passes more easily when it is framed around a concrete, visible benefit rather than the cost it imposes, because the salient gain mobilises support while the pain is what opponents naturally emphasise.

nodes.title: Sanction Regimes Must Match the Offender Population's Composition
nodes.claim: An enforcement strategy works by targeting the dominant offender type: broad, low-severity deterrence when most offenders are conditional, and reserved harsh penalties for the residual persistent minority.

nodes.title: Scale Economics Keep the Incumbent Method Alive
nodes.claim: Even a superior synthetic route stays niche while it cannot match the volume the incumbent supplies at the required unit cost.

nodes.title: Scale-Up Rate, Not Ultimate Capacity, Sets the Timeline
nodes.claim: For a programme that must reach very large scale, the completion date is governed almost entirely by how fast capacity doubles, not by the size of the eventual endpoint or by the resources ultimately available. Growth rate is the variable to optimize; total capacity is usually not binding.

nodes.title: Scaling a System Surfaces New Problems Requiring New Inventions
nodes.claim: Each extension of a growing system surfaces novel failure modes that demand new component inventions, so scaling is itself a driver of invention.

nodes.title: Scaling a Technology Is a Distinct Problem From Inventing It
nodes.claim: Producing a material cheaply at industrial volume requires wholly different skills, capital, and mindsets than discovering it, so success at invention does not carry over to success at scale.

nodes.title: Scaling Compute, Data, and Parameters Drives Capability Gains
nodes.claim: Adding more computation, training data, and model parameters to the same architecture produces large, often qualitative jumps in capability without new conceptual breakthroughs.

nodes.title: Scaling Drives Costs Down a Learning Curve So Guaranteed Volume Substitutes for Waiting
nodes.claim: New technologies are expensive at first and only get cheap as cumulative production grows, so buying early volume at a premium pulls a product down its cost curve faster - an investment in future affordability rather than just current output.

nodes.title: Scarcity Selects Against the Hardest-to-Accommodate
nodes.claim: When the buffer of spare space tightens, the people pushed out first are those hardest to live with, not simply the poorest.

nodes.title: Science and Invention Co-Evolve
nodes.claim: Science and invention are reciprocal, not sequential. Rather than a clean one-way handoff from research to engineering, the two co-evolve: science gives inventors a conceptual toolbox, inventors experiment at and beyond its frontier, and their working-but-unexplained results feed back to pull science forward. Progress is fastest where the two are tightly coupled.

nodes.title: Scientific Applications Are Unforeseeable
nodes.claim: The practical applications of basic scientific discovery are long-term and largely impossible to foresee, and the reverse path is even harder: you cannot reliably specify a practical goal and deduce which science to pursue to reach it.

nodes.title: Seed Preconditions, Don't Pick Winners
nodes.claim: Governments cannot reliably manufacture innovation hubs by designating a target location or technology and spending to make it happen. What works is funding the general preconditions — talent inflows, housing, a neutral portfolio of research support — and amplifying clusters once they begin to emerge organically.

nodes.title: Selection on Visible Traits Drives Inbreeding and Recessive Harm
nodes.claim: Breeding within a narrow set of 'acceptable-looking' families concentrates the gene pool and spreads harmful recessives that surface generations later.

nodes.title: Selective Behavioral Uptake Limits Social Solutions
nodes.claim: A solution that depends on voluntary behaviour change reaches only those willing to change, so its population impact is capped by uptake regardless of efficacy.

nodes.title: Selectivity Separates a Drug's Benefit From Its Side Effects
nodes.claim: Re-engineering a compound to hit only its intended target removes off-target effects that made the original molecule clinically unusable.

nodes.title: Separating a Composite Asset Into Priced Components Is Often Impossible
nodes.claim: When an asset trades only as a bundle, there is no market price for its components, so any policy that must value one component in isolation is administratively unworkable.

nodes.title: Serendipitous Adjacency Generates Ideas Directed Search Cannot
nodes.claim: Physically browsing an unfiltered array surfaces unexpected juxtapositions that a targeted query would never return, catalyzing novel combinations - so optimizing purely for search efficiency eliminates the productive noise from which breakthroughs emerge.

nodes.title: Serial Copying Degrades a Record Into Fragments and Variants
nodes.claim: When an original is never preserved and only serial copies survive, the record degrades into fragments and conflicting variants, so the surviving text is a reconstruction with irreducible uncertainty rather than a faithful transcript.

nodes.title: Shared Infrastructure Exploits Diversity of Simultaneous Demand
nodes.claim: Networking many buildings' heating and cooling loads together — rather than serving each in isolation — lets surplus heat rejected by one use (e.g. an ice rink's cooling load) offset a deficit in another (e.g. an adjacent building's heating load), multiplying system-wide efficiency beyond what any single building's equipment could achieve alone.

nodes.title: Shifting Requirements Mid-Development Compound Delay and Cost
nodes.claim: When a regulator adds requirements after a development programme is under way, the cost is not the new studies alone but everything that has to be rebuilt around them: funding rounds reopened, staff rehired, manufacturing halted and restarted, and the whole schedule pushed out by far more than the studies themselves take.

nodes.title: Shipping an Improvable Solution Beats Waiting for the Perfect One
nodes.claim: Refusing to launch until a solution is complete and objection-proof forfeits all the marginal good it could do in the meantime; a solution that helps at the margin and improves over time dominates a theoretically perfect one that ships too late or never.

nodes.title: Short Time-to-Resolution Drives Gambling Demand
nodes.claim: Bettors overwhelmingly prefer wagers that resolve quickly, so long-horizon or never-resolving contracts attract little volume regardless of how important the underlying event is.

nodes.title: Short-Term Optimization Erodes the Resource It Exploits
nodes.claim: Maximising a target by exploiting only the current best units degrades the underlying resource — genetic diversity, a stock, a commons — threatening future output.

nodes.title: Side Effects Cap the Population an Intervention Can Reach
nodes.claim: Even a broadly protective intervention cannot be deployed to healthy or low-risk populations if it carries meaningful risks, because the risk-benefit calculus only favors those already sick enough.

nodes.title: Simplicity Enables Reliable Repair
nodes.claim: Simple systems are more reliable not because they fail less in the abstract but because, when they do fail, they can be understood and repaired with the materials and knowledge at hand; complexity multiplies both the ways a system can break and the resources needed to fix it.

nodes.title: Skills Honed Against One Class of Agent Transfer to Another
nodes.claim: A cognitive or practical capacity selected for in dealings with one class of agent does not stay confined to it. Because the underlying operation is general — model the other, predict it, signal to it — the capacity gets redeployed against agents it was never selected against, including agents of a completely different kind.

nodes.title: Small Measurement Biases Compound Into Large Distributive Stakes
nodes.claim: When a metric is wired into indexed payments, a tiny per-period bias accumulates over time into enormous transfers, turning an apparently trivial parameter into a high-stakes distributive question.

nodes.title: Small-Animal Bias in Moral Intuition
nodes.claim: Humans systematically underweight moral harm when it is distributed across many small, less salient entities rather than concentrated in a few large, identifiable ones.

nodes.title: Small-Scale Opt-In Rezoning Bypasses the Jurisdiction-Level Veto
nodes.claim: Letting a single building's owners opt into denser zoning removes the decision from the municipal political arena where swing voters and organized opponents block development.

nodes.title: Social Norms Function as Moral Costs Within Rational Choice
nodes.claim: Community disapproval enters an offender's cost-benefit calculation as a real, quantifiable cost, so 'norms' and 'incentives' are the same thing viewed from two angles rather than competing explanations of behaviour.

nodes.title: Sociopathy as a Frequency-Dependent High-Risk Strategy
nodes.claim: A rare exploitative behavioural type can thrive precisely because most others cooperate, making sociopathy a frequency-dependent adaptation rather than mere disorder.

nodes.title: Some Technologies Structurally Favor Defense Over Offense
nodes.claim: The same technical mechanism that enables an attack can be easier to reverse than to launch, so a technology can be inherently biased toward defense - lowering, rather than raising, the risk from misuse.

nodes.title: Specification Gaming Optimizes the Letter of a Goal Against Its Spirit
nodes.claim: A system that maximizes a specified objective will exploit the exact wording of that objective, producing behavior the designer never intended because the true intent was underspecified.

nodes.title: Specificity Trades Efficacy Against Robustness
nodes.claim: A highly specific intervention gains precision -- hitting only its target and sparing everything else -- but loses robustness, because it fails entirely if the target is misidentified or shifts. Specificity is simultaneously the advantage and the fragility of a tool.

nodes.title: Specifying the Product Without Specifying the Producer Preserves Technological Neutrality
nodes.claim: Defining a target product profile - what 'great' looks like - while staying agnostic about who builds it or how lets the market discover both the technology and the inventor, capturing the benefit of competition instead of a funder's bet on one approach.

nodes.title: Speed From Concept to Launch Compounds Because Windows Close and Learning Is in the Doing
nodes.claim: Moving fast from concept to launch matters because opportunities are time-sensitive and most learning comes from execution rather than theorizing, so the cost of delay and the risk of a closing window can outweigh a more complete or elegant design.

nodes.title: Spending Other People's Money Weakens Cost Discipline
nodes.claim: When the body that specifies a project does not bear its cost, it demands features it would never buy with its own budget, inflating spending.

nodes.title: Split Incentives Block Efficiency Investment When Payer and Decision-Maker Diverge
nodes.claim: When the party who chooses a technology (e.g. a landlord installing a heating system) is not the party who pays its ongoing operating costs (e.g. a tenant's utility bills), efficient-but-costlier options are systematically under-chosen relative to what would benefit the parties jointly.

nodes.title: Spontaneous Order Encodes Dispersed Knowledge Better Than Top-Down Design
nodes.claim: Complex systems like cities self-organise through decentralised adaptation that aggregates dispersed local knowledge no central designer could gather.

nodes.title: Sprawl Is Produced by Regulation Rather Than Revealed Preference
nodes.claim: Low-density, car-dependent development is commonly read as what people want and what developers therefore build. It is substantially an artefact of the rules - minimum lot sizes, setbacks, open space and parking requirements - which mandate land consumption per dwelling regardless of demand.

nodes.title: Staged Deployment With Off-Ramps Manages Catastrophic Uncertainty
nodes.claim: Deploying a risky intervention in escalating stages, each measured before the next and reversible if results alarm, lets a society act under deep uncertainty without risking a catastrophic all-at-once error.

nodes.title: Stagnation Locks In Standing Risk
nodes.claim: Halting growth to "play it safe" does not lower existential risk; it freezes society at its current elevated level of risk indefinitely, so that a sufficiently bad event eventually becomes a near-certainty.

nodes.title: Staking Money Weights Opinions by Confidence
nodes.claim: A betting market improves on a simple poll or average because each participant's view enters the estimate in proportion to the money they are willing to risk on it. Those who know more and are more certain buy more, so the resulting price is a confidence-weighted aggregate rather than a headcount — and in a market where contracts pay a fixed sum on resolution, that price reads directly as a probability.

nodes.title: Standardized Replicable Designs Lower Unit Cost via Learning
nodes.claim: Reusing one standardised design across many units simplifies engineering and lets crews improve with repetition, lowering unit cost relative to bespoke design.

nodes.title: State Capacity as General-Purpose Capability
nodes.claim: State capacity is a government's ability to execute tasks reliably, quickly, and at scale across domains (infrastructure, health, law, crisis response).

nodes.title: State Capacity Grows Through Conflict and Crisis
nodes.claim: Major expansions of state capacity are often driven by external threat or internal crisis, which temporarily aligns elite incentives, lowers resistance to taxation and legitimizes centralization. War has historically been the most reliable catalyst.

nodes.title: State Capacity Is Constrained by Revenue Collection
nodes.claim: A state's ability to govern is bounded by its ability to raise, secure and administer revenue. Policies require enforcement, enforcement requires agents, and agents require payment - so where collection is costly, leaky or politically contested, state action is limited regardless of what the ruler intends.

nodes.title: Static Approval Regimes Misfit Rapidly-Evolving Products
nodes.claim: Regulatory systems built to approve a fixed, one-off product handle poorly a class of products that is vast, combinatorial, and constantly updated; treating each variant as a brand-new entity imposes prohibitive costs and blocks otherwise valuable interventions.

nodes.title: Static Publication Slows Error Correction
nodes.claim: Publishing science as static, paywalled prose — rather than as living documents with shared data and code — makes errors slow and costly to detect and fix, and lets flawed results propagate through the citation network for years.

nodes.title: Stationary Commerce Enables Specialization and Parallel Throughput
nodes.claim: When merchants stop travelling with their goods and trade from a fixed base, trade splits into specialised roles that can run in parallel, multiplying throughput.

nodes.title: Stock Damage Requires Removal, Not Just Flow Reduction
nodes.claim: When harm is caused by an accumulated stock rather than by the current rate of emission, halting the flow only stops the stock from growing - it does not reduce it. Any policy target defined on the flow (zero emissions, net zero, phase-out) is therefore structurally incapable of restoring the prior state, and remediation requires a separate removal process operating on the stock itself.

nodes.title: Storability Cancels the Intermittency Penalty of a Variable Input
nodes.claim: When the output of an intermittent process can be cheaply stored, the intermittency of its input stops mattering, so a variable power source becomes as useful as a steady one for that task.

nodes.title: Storable Concentrated Immobile Assets Increase the Payoff to Predation
nodes.claim: Storable, concentrated, and immobile wealth raises both the reward and the feasibility of raiding, so the shift to such assets increases predatory violence.

nodes.title: Structural Honesty Is a Modern Ideology, Not a Historical Norm
nodes.claim: The principle that a good building's outward appearance must honestly express its underlying structure is a modern (largely modernist) ideology, not a timeless standard. The actual history of architecture is overwhelmingly one of divergence between structural appearance and reality.

nodes.title: Studying a Hazard by Creating It Can Have Negative Expected Value
nodes.claim: Investigating a danger by actually instantiating it converts a hypothetical risk into a real one, so the speculative knowledge gained may not justify the concrete catastrophic downside created.

nodes.title: Subsidies Capitalize Into Prices When Supply Is Inelastic
nodes.claim: A demand subsidy for a fixed-stock asset is captured as a windfall by existing owners and bid into the price rather than expanding output or helping intended buyers.

nodes.title: Subsidies Funded by Bailouts Change Who Pays, Not How Much
nodes.claim: A consumer subsidy financed by general taxation or recurring bailouts does not reduce the real resource cost of the good — it only reroutes payment from the meter to the tax bill, so citizens still bear the full cost while losing the incentive information that a cost-reflective price would have carried.

nodes.title: Substitutability Determines Feasibility of Phase-Out
nodes.claim: How easily a harmful input can be eliminated depends on whether good substitutes exist and how embedded the input is: an industry-specific harm with available replacements is tractable; an economy-wide one woven through long-lived infrastructure is not.

nodes.title: Substituting a Cheap Measurement for an Expensive One Unlocks Scale
nodes.claim: Reformulating a problem so its required input is cheap to obtain rather than costly removes the binding constraint on how far a method can be extended.

nodes.title: Suffering Footprint Is Non-Intuitive
nodes.claim: Human moral intuitions about harm fail when suffering is distributed across many small, short-lived entities rather than a few large identifiable ones. As a result, diets and choices perceived as ethical can cause substantially more aggregate suffering than choices perceived as callous.

nodes.title: Sunset Clauses Force Rules to Re-Earn Their Existence
nodes.claim: A rule that expires unless actively renewed must periodically be re-justified by someone willing to bear the organizational cost of renewing it. Rules that are still wanted survive; rules that persist only through inertia lapse, which prevents the indefinite accumulation of restrictions.

nodes.title: Supermajority Rules Overcome Holdouts
nodes.claim: Replacing unanimity with a qualified-majority trigger that can compel dissenters dissolves the holdout problem, where a single obstructer can block a change everyone else wants.

nodes.title: Suppressing Supply Displaces the Residents It Aims to Protect
nodes.claim: When demand for a location rises and new construction is blocked, incoming higher-income buyers outbid existing residents for the fixed stock, so supply restriction accelerates the displacement it was meant to prevent.

nodes.title: Surrogate Endpoints Trade Speed for Blind Spots
nodes.claim: Approving interventions on biomarkers rather than outcomes accelerates development but means real effects on the outcomes we care about are discovered only later, sometimes reversing expectations.

nodes.title: Survival Implies a Low Background Catastrophe Rate
nodes.claim: The mere fact that a long-lived civilization (or species) exists places an upper bound on the rate of the natural catastrophes that could have ended it: if such events were common, we almost certainly wouldn't be here to observe them.

nodes.title: Survivorship Bias Distorts the Record When Only One Vantage Survives
nodes.claim: When all surviving accounts come from a single, often hostile or self-interested vantage, the reconstructed picture is systematically skewed, and recovering a suppressed viewpoint would materially correct it.

nodes.title: Survivorship Bias Inflates Perceived Quality of the Past
nodes.claim: When the surviving members of a past population are non-random — durable, valued, or beautiful things survive at higher rates — judging the whole past by its survivors systematically overestimates its typical quality.

nodes.title: Symbolic Attributes Add Market Value Independent of Performance
nodes.claim: A product can command attention or a premium through the meaning it signals - environmental virtue, artisanal origin - rather than any gain in function, cost, or quality, so symbolic value can substitute for and disguise the absence of real improvement.

nodes.title: System Analysis Fails Beyond a Few Interacting Parts
nodes.claim: Formal systems analysis works only under narrow conditions — a static system with few parts that can be examined closely and fixed through repeated attempts; beyond that it breeds false confidence rather than understanding.

nodes.title: Tacit Knowledge Transmits via Demonstration
nodes.claim: Much valuable know-how is tacit — hard to put into words — and historically had to pass person-to-person through apprenticeship or family. Recorded demonstration (video) lets that tacit knowledge be transmitted at scale and preserved indefinitely, widening who can acquire elite technique.

nodes.title: Tacit Qualities Require Physical Access That Documentation Cannot Convey
nodes.claim: Some attributes of a thing can only be learned through direct sensory or hands-on encounter, so digitizing its description omits the information that actually drives its use - which is why physical collections gain value as the world goes digital.

nodes.title: Target-Agnostic Surveillance Detects Unknown Threats
nodes.claim: Detection systems that require knowing what to look for are structurally blind to novel hazards; only methods that scan for anything can serve as an early warning for the genuinely new.

nodes.title: Targeting Interventions Requires Locational Data
nodes.claim: You cannot efficiently fix a problem you cannot locate. Even with money and political will, interventions stall or waste resources when the basic data — where the hazard is — is missing or incomplete; building that data is often the binding constraint.

nodes.title: Tax and Subsidy Distortions Misallocate Supply
nodes.claim: Tax reliefs and subsidies aimed at stimulating construction can misallocate it — producing lots of building where it is politically designated but not needed, and too little where demand is real — because the incentive rewards the act of building rather than meeting demand.

nodes.title: Technical Feasibility Does Not Guarantee Substitution
nodes.claim: Being able to make a product a new way does not mean the new way displaces the old; adoption is gated by separate economic, regulatory, and complexity barriers.

nodes.title: Technology Adoption Is Gated by Local Constraints
nodes.claim: A clearly superior, labor-saving technology can fail to spread for a long time because adoption is gated by environmental, technical, and economic constraints — not, as is often assumed, by cultural attachment or irrational preference.

nodes.title: Temporary Surges Are Cheaper Than Permanent Deficits
nodes.claim: A one-off "fiscal surge" — a temporary jump in borrowing for an extraordinary, time-limited purpose — carries a far smaller long-run burden than a permanent increase in the deficit, because economies rebound after temporary shocks and the spike's relative weight decays under favorable r − g.

nodes.title: The As-If Game in Science
nodes.claim: In some fields, researchers tacitly agree to accept prior published results as true and build on them — an improvisational "yes, and" — so that challenging a finding is treated as a hostile, almost illegitimate move. Errors then compound through citation rather than being corrected.

nodes.title: The Binding Constraint Lies Upstream of the Visible Bottleneck
nodes.claim: When the downstream process is already cheap and reliable, gains come from relieving the true scarce input, not from improving the visible procedure.

nodes.title: The False Tradeoff Between Reproducibility and Innovation
nodes.claim: Improving scientific reproducibility and increasing scientific innovation are widely believed to trade off — tighter quality control supposedly stifles creativity. In fact they share a common cause (the demand for predictable positive results and deference to consensus), so the right reforms improve both at once.

nodes.title: The Fertility Gap
nodes.claim: People in developed countries have fewer children than they say they want: stated desired fertility exceeds actual fertility. Because the gap is driven by prosaic, removable costs (housing, childcare, career timing) rather than a preference against children, fertility can be raised by lowering those barriers without trying to change anyone's values.

nodes.title: The Hold-Up Problem Deters Relationship-Specific Investment
nodes.claim: When one party must sink a large irreversible investment before bargaining with a buyer who has substantial market power, that buyer can renegotiate the price downward afterwards, since the investment is already sunk. Anticipating this, the investor does not invest at all - and the loss is the project, not merely the surplus.

nodes.title: The Precautionary Principle Can Increase Net Risk
nodes.claim: Aggressively applying the precautionary principle — blocking or slowing action "out of an abundance of caution" — can raise net risk rather than lower it, because the foregone capability and delayed responses cost more safety than the avoided hazard.

nodes.title: The Same Infrastructure That Provides a Good Can Weaponize It
nodes.claim: Infrastructure built to deliver a benefit — storage, power, flow control — simultaneously creates the capability to withhold or weaponize that benefit, so provision and coercion are two uses of one asset.

nodes.title: The Storage Medium Selects Which Contents Get Represented
nodes.claim: The physical or institutional constraints of a repository bias its holdings toward what it can accommodate, systematically excluding otherwise important items and quietly distorting perception of the whole field.

nodes.title: Theory Lets Indirect Evidence Substitute for Replication
nodes.claim: A unified theoretical framework lets a wide variety of different studies serve as checks on each other — supporting or contradicting the shared theory — so a field can build confidence without relying on direct replications, which the priority system underincentivizes.

nodes.title: Thin Markets Are Manipulable and Uninformative
nodes.claim: A market price is only an informative aggregate of belief if enough capital is trading in it. In a low-liquidity market a single well-funded participant can move the price cheaply and no one has enough at stake to trade the distortion away, so the price reports manipulation or noise rather than the crowd's judgment. Liquidity is therefore a precondition for a market to function as an information device at all.

nodes.title: Thin Markets Leave Valuable Products Undeveloped
nodes.claim: Low revenue potential combined with regulator unfamiliarity means no one develops a product, regardless of how much it is needed, because the payoff cannot justify the fixed cost of getting it approved.

nodes.title: Tiered Staged Funding Bridges Evidence and Scale-Up
nodes.claim: A single funder can span the pipeline from unproven idea to large-scale rollout by offering escalating grant tiers gated on demonstrated results, funding both the creation of initial evidence and the scaling of what works.

nodes.title: Tinkering Plateaus Without a Scientific Base
nodes.claim: Practical technological progress can advance for a while through ad-hoc tinkering and trial-and-error, but without an underlying scientific understanding it eventually plateaus — because tinkerers lack a correct model of the goal and of what counts as success.

nodes.title: Titling and Consolidation Raise Land Productivity
nodes.claim: Converting fragmented, collectively held plots into contiguous, individually titled farms sharply increases agricultural output.

nodes.title: Tolerance for a Hazard Falls as Its Offsetting Benefit Disappears
nodes.claim: Society's willingness to bear a known hazard depends on the benefit it delivers; when substitutes make that benefit redundant, the same hazard becomes intolerable even if its intrinsic danger is unchanged.

nodes.title: Tractable Local Workarounds Crowd Out Systemic Reform
nodes.claim: Funders and reformers systematically prefer small, self-contained interventions that can be started immediately over the systemic policy change that would actually resolve the problem, because the local project is tractable, attributable, and politically safe — so effort concentrates where it is easiest to deploy rather than where leverage is highest.

nodes.title: Trait Persistence Does Not Imply Pathology
nodes.claim: The persistence of a trait in a population is compatible with both dysfunction and adaptation. Prevalence alone carries no information about whether something is a disorder, so the existence of a widespread harmful trait is not evidence that it is a disease.

nodes.title: Transaction Costs Shape Organizational Form
nodes.claim: Organizations internalize activities when the costs of coordinating them through markets exceed the costs of doing so through authority. The boundary of the firm - or the state, or a research institution - is set by that comparison rather than by strategy or ideology.

nodes.title: Transparency Substitutes for Trust in Delegated Authority
nodes.claim: Binding requirements to publish and be scrutinised legitimise authority granted to unelected officials, by making their decisions visible and reviewable rather than asking the public to simply trust them.

nodes.title: Transport Costs Determine the Reach of Central Authority
nodes.claim: A government can only govern where it can move people, money and force. High transport costs therefore cap state capacity directly, producing fragmented regional markets, autonomous local power and a centre that cannot enforce its own rules beyond a limited radius.

nodes.title: Treating the Regulated System Beats Fighting Its Output
nodes.claim: When an outcome is produced by a regulated control system, durable change comes from resetting the system's target, not from forcing its output against the regulator. Effective obesity drugs work by acting on the brain's fat-regulation circuitry (lowering the setpoint), not by sheer appetite suppression willpower-style.

nodes.title: Trial Cost Caps the Diversity of Approaches Attempted
nodes.claim: When the cost of testing a product is enormous, only the largest players attempt it and only conventional-looking approaches get tried, because no one will risk a huge sum on a modality that will look foolish if it fails.

nodes.title: Two-Sided Uncertainty Blocks Investment Without a Credible Commitment
nodes.claim: When producers doubt buyers will actually purchase at scale and buyers doubt producers will deliver quality, neither side makes the large up-front commitment needed, so a mutually beneficial market fails to form.

nodes.title: Uncontrolled Background Exposure Biases Estimates of a Hazard's Effect
nodes.claim: When members of a study's control group are unknowingly exposed to the hazard being studied, researchers underestimate both the harm to those "unexposed" and the marginal risk of further exposure.

nodes.title: Underpowered Studies Can Be Worse Than None
nodes.claim: A study with too little statistical power to detect a plausible effect can be worse than no study at all: it yields an inconclusive result that both sides misinterpret as supporting their position, hardening beliefs and misleading policy.

nodes.title: Undiversified Wealth Makes Owners Veto Positive-Expected-Value Change
nodes.claim: When most of a household's wealth sits in a single asset, its owner rationally refuses changes that raise expected value but add variance to that asset's price. The veto is not irrational or merely selfish — it is correct portfolio behaviour for someone who cannot diversify.

nodes.title: Unexpected Inflation Transfers Wealth From Creditors to Debtors
nodes.claim: Rapid, unanticipated inflation erodes the real value of fixed nominal debt, rescuing over-leveraged borrowers at the expense of savers and lenders.

nodes.title: Unified Theory Raises the Base Rate of True Hypotheses
nodes.claim: A good, unified theory improves the prior probability that the hypotheses a field tests are true. Because the share of published (and even replicated) findings that are real depends heavily on this base rate, theory that steers researchers toward likelier-true hypotheses is one of the most powerful levers on a field's reliability.

nodes.title: Uniting Local Opposition Into a Single Coalition Defeats Divide-and-Rule
nodes.claim: A government can usually buy off, relocate, or wait out a single local objection to a project, but when many separate local groups combine into one campaign, the only settlement that satisfies every member is cancelling the project outright — coalition formation converts a series of manageable local vetoes into one unmanageable collective veto.

nodes.title: Unobserved Failures Bias Inference About Selection Processes
nodes.claim: When only successes are recorded - funded grants, published papers, granted patents - and the failures (rejected applicants, unpublished projects, untrained students) are invisible, the available data systematically distorts what can be learned about the process that produced them.

nodes.title: Unprecedented Components Force Vertical Integration
nodes.claim: When the parts a product needs do not yet exist as tradeable goods, there is no supplier to buy them from and no contract that can specify them, so the innovator must manufacture them in-house. Novelty, not strategy, is what makes the firm vertically integrated.

nodes.title: Unquestioning Trust Erodes Scientific Reliability
nodes.claim: Treating scientific claims with implicit, unquestioning trust — lowering the barrier of monitoring, challenging, and checking — removes the very scrutiny that makes science reliable, so excessive trust is self-undermining rather than warranted.

nodes.title: Up-Front Investigation De-Risks Uncertain Execution
nodes.claim: Spending early on investigation — surveys, expert study, ground truth — buys certainty that prevents far costlier failures during execution.

nodes.title: Upsizing a Design Adds Complexity That Erodes Its Scale Economies
nodes.claim: Making a unit bigger to capture economies of scale can backfire when the larger size forces added subsystems and integration work whose cost grows faster than output, eroding the expected savings.

nodes.title: Upstream Prevention Beats Downstream Repair
nodes.claim: Acting on the root cause upstream is often less invasive and less risky than repairing its downstream consequences after they occur.

nodes.title: Users Make Their Own Inputs When Markets Fail to Supply Them
nodes.claim: When no supplier offers a needed ingredient, sophisticated users produce it themselves, and successful home-brews can turn into commercial products and new market categories.

nodes.title: Uses That Tolerate Heterogeneity Unlock Low-Value Waste Streams
nodes.claim: The share of a waste stream that gets recovered is set less by collection than by sorting cost: recycling routes that require a pure input can only absorb the fraction worth separating, so the low-value remainder is landfilled.
