An end use that tolerates a mixed, unsorted input removes the sorting step from the cost structure and makes exactly that discarded fraction economically recoverable.

nodes.title: Vaccination Is the Only Intervention That Achieves Eradication
nodes.claim: Among approaches to infection — prevention, containment, cure, symptom treatment, vaccination — only vaccination has ever driven a disease to extinction, because it is durable and does not require ongoing universal effort.

nodes.title: Vague Rules Deter Investment by Raising Approval Uncertainty
nodes.claim: When rules are kept deliberately vague to preserve a regulator's discretion, firms cannot predict whether an investment will be approved, and that uncertainty deters the investment even when the rule's intent is benign.

nodes.title: Value Capture Lets Infrastructure Pay for Itself
nodes.claim: Infrastructure raises the value of the land it serves; if the public body that built it is allowed to capture part of that uplift — through taxes on the enhanced value, or by permitting development that would not otherwise be legal — the investment can finance itself rather than competing with other spending.

nodes.title: Variant Beliefs Recruit Aligned Talent
nodes.claim: An organization that publicly articulates a contrarian or "variant" vision of the future recruits precisely the people who share that vision — gaining a focused, motivated workforce without having to persuade the wider world, because the bet is ultimately settled by technology and economics, not consensus.

nodes.title: Verifiable Scarcity Creates a Digital Store of Value
nodes.claim: A digital asset with credibly fixed supply and cheap direct transfer can function as a store of value — "digital gold" — attractive precisely as a hedge against the debasement of government-issued money.

nodes.title: Vernacular Arts Must Be Executable by the Median Practitioner
nodes.claim: In a field where most output is produced by ordinary practitioners rather than by a handful of exceptional ones, a style should be judged by what it produces in average hands. A style that yields masterpieces from masters and disasters from everyone else is worse in aggregate than one that yields competent work from anyone.

nodes.title: Viewers Supply Context From Their Own Knowledge and History
nodes.claim: Viewers complete their experience of an object using their own knowledge and history, so groups with different backgrounds genuinely experience the same object differently.

nodes.title: Voluntary Inconvenience Becomes a Status Good Under Abundance
nodes.claim: Once material needs are trivially met, deliberately effortful, time-consuming, or uncomfortable pursuits become desirable status and meaning goods.

nodes.title: Vote-Buy Gap in Ethical Consumption
nodes.claim: People express ethical preferences politically while failing to enact them as consumers.

nodes.title: Vulnerability Plus Offensive Capacity Makes Conflict Catastrophic
nodes.claim: When a species is both fragile and highly capable of offence, every conflict is potentially catastrophic, which selects for strong restraint and norms.

nodes.title: Wealth Raises the Value of Life
nodes.claim: As people grow richer, they place a higher value on their own lives and are willing to sacrifice a larger fraction of income to avoid death — so wealth raises the demand for safety.

nodes.title: Weighting Procurement on Value Not Lowest Bid Prevents Underbidding Games
nodes.claim: Scoring tenders on technical merit and time as well as price, rather than awarding to the lowest bid, deters strategic under-bidding that later explodes into overruns.

nodes.title: What a Society Remembers Encodes Its Theory of Causation
nodes.claim: The events a culture makes memorable and canonical encode an implicit theory of what drives change; the salience of certain dates is not neutral but reflects and reinforces a belief about which forces shape the world.

nodes.title: When the Median Voter Owns the Asset, Shortage Loses Political Salience
nodes.claim: Once a majority of voters own the asset that is in short supply, the shortage stops being a political problem and becomes a political asset, because the median voter's wealth rises with the scarcity. The people harmed — non-owners and future entrants — are a minority, are dispersed, and in the case of future entrants cannot vote at all.

nodes.title: Zero-Sum Instruments Cannot Attract Long-Term Savings
nodes.claim: Savers avoid negative- or zero-sum vehicles because positive-sum assets that fund real production reliably grow wealth over the long run, so a betting market cannot draw the patient capital that deepens it.

nodes.title: Build State Capacity by Building Charter Cities
nodes.claim: State capacity — the ability to deliver public goods, enforce rules, and attract investment — is the binding constraint on development, not a shortage of good policy ideas or resources. Charter cities can accelerate capacity-building by creating blank-slate governance zones with devolved authority that bypass institutional sclerosis and entrenched rent coalitions, and can import working institutions wholesale rather than reforming dysfunctional ones.
nodes.author: Mark Lutter & Jeffrey Mason

nodes.title: Epidemic Disease and the State
nodes.claim: Epidemic response reveals underlying state capacity and its relationship with civil society. The apparent trade-off between liberty and public health is real but not fixed: it can be "bent" by a more effective (not necessarily larger) state and by a civil society aligned with it. Western floundering on Covid-19 reflects pre-existing institutional pathologies — rent-seeking, sclerosis, and elite overproduction — rather than the shock of the disease itself.
nodes.author: Mark Koyama

nodes.title: How to Build a State
nodes.claim: Early states lacked bureaucratic capacity and were therefore forced to govern through delegation, corruption, and bargaining with private power; modern state capacity emerged slowly through institutionalized legitimacy, especially via parliaments that could raise taxes, change policy, and undo predecessors' deals.

nodes.title: Practical Veganism

nodes.author: Samuel Watling

nodes.title: Why we stopped building cut and cover
nodes.claim: For nearly a century, urban subways were built by "cut and cover" — digging an open trench, building the tunnel, then covering it — because it was far cheaper than boring. nodes.author: Brian Potter

nodes.title: Britain's forgotten financial crisis
nodes.claim: Britain's fastest-ever house-price growth came not in the 2020s but in 1971-73, a 70% real spike, and the episode is a clean natural experiment showing there is no alternative to building. nodes.title: Gentrification as a housing problem
nodes.claim: Gentrification is a real problem for the people it pushes out, but its root cause is inflexible housing supply, and the popular remedies - blocking new development, downzoning, rent control - make it worse. Where supply is constrained, incoming higher-income demand outbids existing residents for a fixed stock, so suppressing construction accelerates the very displacement it means to prevent. Rent control shrinks and degrades the controlled stock and allocates it by queue and connection; …
nodes.author: Anya Martin

nodes.title: Getting materials out of the lab
nodes.claim: Inventing a new material is only the first and easier step; getting it into mass production and use is a distinct, harder problem that most materials never survive. nodes.author: Benjamin Reinhardt

nodes.title: How the war on drunk driving was won
nodes.claim: Deterrence and social norms are not rival explanations of why drunk driving collapsed; they are two views of the same process. nodes.author: Ben Adler

nodes.title: The beauty of concrete
nodes.claim: Modern buildings are austere and unornamented not because ornament became unaffordable, but because taste changed. nodes.author: Samuel Hughes

nodes.title: Why prediction markets aren't popular
nodes.claim: Prediction markets are largely legal, yet they stay thin and unpopular - and the reason is a lack of genuine demand, not prohibition. nodes.author: Nan Ransohoff

nodes.title: Lab-grown diamonds
nodes.claim: Synthetic diamonds are now purer, more beautiful, more durable, and vastly cheaper than mined stones, made by two independent routes - high-pressure high-temperature (HPHT) synthesis, which mimics the Earth's mantle, and chemical vapour deposition (CVD), a gas-phase process never seen in nature. nodes.author: Javid Lakha

nodes.title: Libraries of matter
nodes.claim: Materials libraries - curated, physical collections of samples that can be touched, handled, and borrowed - are a decentralized institution for spurring material progress by making the tacit, sensory qualities of materials available in a way spec sheets and databases cannot. nodes.title: The ultra-selfish gene
nodes.claim: Ten years ago the CRISPR/Cas9 gene drive gave humanity a way to rewrite or eliminate an entire wild species by making an edit that copies itself to nearly 100 percent of offspring, and applied to the few Anopheles gambiae subspecies that carry malaria it could end a disease that kills over half a million people a year. …
nodes.author: Mathias Kirk Bonde

nodes.title: Where inflation comes from
nodes.claim: How a society measures inflation is not a settled technical fact but an evolving, politically contested construction, and small methodological choices materially change how prosperous a nation believes itself to be. nodes.author: Carola Conces Binder

nodes.title: Animals as Chemical Factories
nodes.claim: For millennia humans have used animals as chemical factories, harvesting molecules (dye, oil, insulin, antivenom, endotoxin reagent, vaccines) from their bodies. Recombinant DNA now makes it technically possible to synthesise almost any such molecule from engineered cells, often at higher purity. nodes.title: How Big Data Created the Modern Dairy Cow
nodes.claim: The US became the world's dominant dairy-genetics power not through superior native cattle but by building a data-collection infrastructure that let breeders select animals on measured productivity rather than appearance or pedigree. nodes.author: Jared Hutchins

nodes.title: How Madrid Built Its Metro Cheaply
nodes.claim: Between 1995 and 2007 Madrid nearly tripled its metro (adding 126 miles) at roughly a tenth of London's or New York's per-mile cost, showing the 'good, fast, cheap: choose two' trilemma is not an iron law. nodes.author: Ben Hopkinson

nodes.title: Machines for Living In
nodes.claim: Modern functionalism went wrong not by emphasising a building's function but by misconstruing 'function' as nonaesthetic utility alone. Properly understood, a building's function is the everyday context in which its actual users experience it, and that context should determine which form makes it beautiful. nodes.author: Ralph S Weir

nodes.title: Progress Unmoored
nodes.claim: While progress on land-based physical infrastructure has stagnated and costs have risen, cruise ships keep breaking size records and falling in real cost. The difference is not technological difficulty, skills, or materials but the regulatory and institutional constraints that land-based projects face and ships at sea escape. Cruise ships are a natural experiment showing that stagnation is a choice of rules, not an inevitability, and that dense, diverse, walkable environments can be desirable and safe.
nodes.author: Michael Hopkins

nodes.title: The World of Tomorrow
nodes.claim: For most of the twentieth century 'the future' was glamorous — an alluring image that focused deep longings onto an idealised escape. But glamour is by nature an illusion that hides trade-offs, so once the futuristic present arrived it lost its mystery, revealed its costs, and provoked a counterculture backlash. Progress can recover its appeal only by abandoning modernism's 'one best way' for a pluralist abundance agenda that supplies a common material substrate for many different versions of the good life.
nodes.author: Virginia Postrel

nodes.title: How Pineapples Got Cheap

nodes.author: Etienne Fortier-Dubois

nodes.title: Steam Networks
nodes.claim: Manhattan's century-old municipal steam network (running since 1882) is an iconic anachronism that survived because it solved the specific problems of a rapidly densifying vertical city — centralising coal logistics, cutting fire risk, and heating skyscrapers — better than on-site boilers. nodes.author: Jamie Rumbelow

nodes.title: The Failure of the Land Value Tax

nodes.title: The Prehistoric Psychopath

nodes.author: John Halstead & Phil Thomson

nodes.title: The Rise and Fall of the Hanseatic League
nodes.claim: The Hanseatic League was a stateless, territory-less coalition of medieval German merchant cities that achieved state-like power — signing treaties, blockading cities, winning wars, and securing tax privileges below even native merchants' — purely through collective bargaining, collective action, and collective security. nodes.author: Agree Ahmed

nodes.title: Brain-Computer Interfaces
nodes.claim: Brain-computer interfaces — systems that read neurons' electrical activity and turn it into commands — are letting paralysed people move cursors, control robotic limbs, and speak, and the first FDA approvals may arrive within five years. nodes.author: Rebecca Hiscott

nodes.title: How One Kiwi Tamed Inflation
nodes.claim: Inflation targeting — now standard central banking — did not come from economic research or expert consensus but from a political gamble: New Zealand Finance Minister Roger Douglas announced explicit inflation goals on television in 1988 to signal commitment, and officials then built a statutory framework (operational independence, a single price-stability mandate, published statements) around it. nodes.author: Oscar Sykes

nodes.title: How to Redraw a City
nodes.claim: Japan faced extreme land fragmentation — crooked premodern cities and postwar reforms that split farmland into tiny plots — yet replanned its cities successfully through "land readjustment": pooling neighbouring plots, redrawing boundaries to carve out roads and parks, selling reserve land to fund the works, and returning each owner a smaller but more valuable plot. Its durability rests on two mechanisms: sharing the uplift evenly, and requiring a supermajority of affected owners to opt in.
nodes.author: Anya Martin

nodes.title: The Bad Science Behind Expensive Nuclear
nodes.claim: Nuclear power is made unaffordable largely by ALARA regulation ("as low as reasonably achievable"), which stems from the Linear No Threshold (LNT) model holding that any radiation dose raises cancer risk and that harm simply accumulates. LNT was built on 1920s-30s fruit-fly experiments and entrenched amid Cold War weapons-testing scandals, yet its scientific basis — ignoring the body's repair capacity and contradicted by low-dose epidemiology — may now be collapsing.
nodes.author: Alex Chalmers

nodes.title: The End of Lead
nodes.claim: Lead has been all but eliminated in rich countries but still poisons much of the developing world, causing an estimated 5.5 million cardiovascular deaths a year and ~1 percent of global GDP in lost potential. Because lead's harm is silent and invisible, it is systematically neglected; but the fix is cheap and well understood — screen blood, find the sources (paint, spices, cosmetics, informal battery recycling), and help manufacturers switch — so eliminating it globally may be surprisingly easy.
nodes.author: Clare Donaldson, Lauren Gilbert & James Hu

nodes.title: The Magic of Through Running
nodes.claim: Nineteenth-century commuter railways terminated at the edge of cities, leaving a "hubless wheel" of lines that never meet. nodes.title: The Daily Grind

nodes.claim: "Systems thinking" promises that careful analysis can design and fix complex systems, but the record shows governments coming off worse because complex systems kick back against intervention (Le Chatelier's Principle, generalized by John Gall). nodes.author: Ed Bradon

nodes.author: Connor Tabarrok

nodes.title: Sunscreen for the Planet
nodes.claim: The world is warming faster than emissions are falling, and carbon removal is nowhere near scale. nodes.author: Daniele Visioni & Dakota Gruener

nodes.author: Deena Mousa

nodes.title: The Death Rays That Guard Life

nodes.title: Why Didn't Suicides Rise During Covid

This paradox — more misery, less suicide — resists every easy explanation (government support, less social stress, means restriction, Durkheim's "coming together"). nodes.title: Asteroid Spotting
nodes.claim: A civilization-ending asteroid impact is a real but extremely rare and now well-managed risk. We can infer its rarity partly from our own survival, and NASA's tracking has found ~95% of >1km near-Earth objects, cutting the chance of a Chicxulub-scale event this century to ~1 in 150 million. nodes.title: Better Eats
nodes.claim: Home kitchens look much as they did in 1960, but cooking has been transformed — not by new appliances but by intangible capital: recipes, techniques, scientific understanding (Harold McGee), and know-how, distributed at scale via YouTube, recipe sites, and social media. nodes.title: Buyers of First Resort
nodes.claim: Innovation policy is dominated by supply-side support (R&D grants, subsidies, patents), but many technologies also need a "Buyer of First Resort" — an entity that creates the first market for a promising but immature product, bridging the gap between development and self-sustaining adoption. nodes.title: How Trust Undermines Science
nodes.claim: Implicit, unquestioning trust in "science" paradoxically undermines it. nodes.title: Natalism for Progressives
nodes.claim: Falling fertility across the developed world (TFR below replacement almost everywhere) is a threat to progress that progressives, not just the nationalist right, should care about: fewer people means fewer ideas, and an aging society becomes risk-averse and short-termist. nodes.title: The Future of Weight Loss
nodes.claim: Obesity long resisted treatment not for lack of effort but because body fat is actively regulated by the brain around a "setpoint" that it defends: diet-induced weight loss triggers a compensatory starvation response (more hunger, lower metabolism, more food reward) — an evolved relic of when weight loss was a mortal threat. nodes.title: The Housing Theory of Everything
nodes.claim: A single problem — too few homes built where people want to live — is an upstream cause of a startling range of Western ills: low productivity and slow growth, inequality (both personal and regional), falling fertility, obesity, climate emissions, financial instability, and even culture-war polarization. nodes.title: Against the Survival of the Prettiest
nodes.claim: Modern buildings really are uglier than old ones, and the fashionable "survivorship bias" rebuttal — that we only think old buildings are beautiful because the ugly ones were demolished — cannot be the main explanation. nodes.title: Parenting as a Public Good
nodes.claim: Children are a positive externality — society benefits from each new generation while the private costs (money, time, career, and uniquely the physical/health toll of pregnancy) fall on parents, disproportionately mothers. nodes.title: Who Cares About Plagiarism
nodes.claim: The pro-plagiarism case (Bob Dylan's "we all do it," Brian Frye's "plagiarism norms are academic rent-seeking," and the Open Science impulse toward "Open Ideas") is seductive but wrong. nodes.title: Why Ireland's Housing Bubble Burst
nodes.claim: Ireland's 2000s housing bubble (prices quadrupled to 2007, then halved by 2012) is used as a Rorschach test, but three popular myths about it are wrong. nodes.title: Why Skyscrapers Are So Short
nodes.claim: Building height is capped by three frontiers that diverge as technology matures: the physical limit (a steel frame could reach ~1 mile), the economic limit (returns are parabolic — office towers optimize around 60–70 storeys), and the legal limit (zoning, FAR, height caps), which springs up to constrain externalities once the economic frontier rises. …

nodes.title: Womb for Improvement
nodes.claim: Pregnancy and childbirth are arduous, dangerous, and for some women impossible; artificial wombs could let more women have children and save premature infants. nodes.author: Aria Babu (Aria Schrecker)

nodes.title: How Polyester Bounced Back
nodes.claim: Polyester's rehabilitation from disco-era punchline to the dominant global textile fiber came not from marketing but from a 1980s paradigm shift that redefined the design problem around the wearer's body (moisture, temperature, comfort) rather than the fabric's inherent properties, unlocking innovations — fleece, moisture-wicking base layers, engineered filament cross-sections, microfibres — that then cascaded from niche outdoor gear into everyday clothing.
nodes.author: Virginia Postrel

nodes.title: Local Warming
nodes.claim: Gas utilities can decarbonize home heating profitably, and without abandoning their workers or low-income customers, by shifting toward networked ground-source heat pump systems ("GeoNetworks") that reuse existing rate-based capital financing and exploit the thermal diversity of many buildings sharing one network — a better path than hydrogen blending, biogas, or leaving customers to convert to individual heat pumps one at a time.
nodes.author: Audrey Schulman

nodes.title: London's Lost Ringways

nodes.author: Michael Dnes

nodes.title: Scientific Slowdown Is Not Inevitable
nodes.claim: The popular "low-hanging fruit" explanation for declining research productivity treats the slowdown as inevitable, but the evidence is equally consistent with an institutional story — that academia's prestige and publication incentives, a shrinking supply of outlier-ability researchers (compounded by declining elite fertility), and environmental pollutants like lead have made us worse at capturing, locating, funding, and staffing research — which would mean the slowdown is reformable rather than destiny.
nodes.author: Ben Southwood

nodes.title: Why Innovation Prizes Fail
nodes.claim: The Longitude Prize's legend is a myth. Innovation prizes rarely spark revolutionary invention out of nowhere; the most effective ones function narrowly — coaxing disclosure of already-known-but-secret solutions, filling gaps left by patents and markets, and depending on sustained developmental funding rather than a single headline lump-sum reward.
nodes.author: Anton Howes

nodes.title: Why We Duel
nodes.claim: Ritualized dueling traditions found across hunter-gatherer and historical societies function primarily to manage and bound interpersonal violence — channeling disputes into rule-governed, survivable contests aimed at reconciliation and legitimation — rather than being simple celebrations of aggression, and evolve new de-escalation conventions whenever the lethality of the weapons involved rises.
nodes.author: William Buckner

nodes.title: Age of the bacteriophage
nodes.claim: As antibiotic resistance rises toward a projected millions of annual deaths by 2050 and the antibiotic pipeline slows, bacteriophages -- viruses that infect bacteria -- offer a revived line of defense. nodes.author: Léa Zinsli

nodes.title: Real peer review has never been tried
nodes.claim: Formal pre-publication peer review is a recent (1970s-80s) and historically contingent institution that journals adopted mainly to manage submission volume and protect reputation, not because it reliably ensures quality. nodes.author: Saloni Dattani

nodes.title: Reclaiming the roads
nodes.claim: Roads were, until recently, shared among a messy mix of pedestrians, horses, carts, and cyclists with no dominant user; today they are almost wholly dominated by cars. nodes.author: Carlton Reid

nodes.title: The decline and fall of the British economy
nodes.claim: Britain's late-Victorian relative economic decline was not caused by entrepreneurial complacency, defective education, or excessive foreign investment, as the standard "declinist" story holds. nodes.author: Davis Kedrosky

nodes.title: The Maintenance Race
nodes.claim: The 1968 Golden Globe solo round-the-world yacht race is best read as a contest of maintenance styles: Robin Knox-Johnston's improvised "make do and mend," Donald Crowhurst's fatal "hope for the best," and Bernard Moitessier's prepared "prepare for the worst." How each sailor anticipated, simplified, and kept up his boat -- not raw speed or willpower -- determined who finished, who quit, and who died. Maintenance, done in advance and continuously, is the hidden discipline behind reliability under stress.
nodes.author: Stewart Brand

nodes.title: We don't have a hundred biases, we have the wrong model
nodes.claim: Behavioral economics has accumulated 200+ "biases" -- deviations from the rational-actor model -- but this is a symptom of using the wrong model, not scientific progress. Like Ptolemaic astronomers adding epicycles, the field needs its own heliocentric revolution: a unified theory of human decision-making. nodes.author: Jason Collins

nodes.title: Advancing antivenom
nodes.claim: Snakebite envenoming kills 81,000-138,000 people a year and disables ~400,000 more, yet the collapse of antivenom supply for poor regions is not a technological inevitability but a product of specific market and government failures. nodes.author: Mathias Kirk Bonde

nodes.title: AI from Superintelligence to ChatGPT
nodes.claim: AI has advanced far faster than skeptics predicted, and recent breakthroughs - deep learning, reinforcement learning, transformers and large language models - lend real credence to the view that increasingly powerful, potentially general intelligence could arrive within decades. nodes.claim: Funders pour money into science while knowing very little about which funding, review, and organizing strategies actually work best. nodes.author: Heidi Williams and Paul Niehaus

nodes.title: History is in the making
nodes.claim: The dominant way of understanding history - as a sequence of political events (wars, revolutions, rulers) - emphasizes the wrong events and misjudges what actually transformed human life. nodes.title: The elements of scientific style
nodes.claim: Scientific papers are poorly written - dense, jargon-laden, acronym-heavy, stylistically flat - and on measurable dimensions have been getting worse for over a century.
